PREFACE 

In this book is presented the Wisconsin law as to private corporations, foreign and domestic, with particular regard to the ordinary business corporation and practical matters concerning its organization and management from legal aspects.

The work is based upon the Wisconsin statutes now in force and upon the decisions of the Supreme Court. In some instances, where Wisconsin authority was lacking, recourse has been had to decisions of other jurisdictions to indicate the trend of authority and probable development of the law here.

The purpose of the work has been to provide a useful and practical manual to guide the practitioner in creating and organizing the corporation and in directing the management of its affairs. It is intended to show what to do, and when and how to do it. To carry out this purpose, forms adequate for every need have been provided. 

Especial attention has also been given to laws controlling foreign corporations, from the granting to the revocation of their licenses, including actions by and against them.

The author wishes particularly to acknowledge courtesies extended by the office of the Secretary of State, and very material aid received from the excellent notes and articles in the Wisconsin and Marquette Law Reviews, and from reports of proceedings of the Wisconsin 

Bar Association. 

January, 1932

JAMES M. HENDERSON

§ 1. Nature Generally of "Corporation." A corpora tion is an artificial creature of the law,¹ substituted for 

1 Northwestern Nat. Ins. Co. v. 

Freedy, 201 Wis. 51, 227 N. W. 

952; Kappers v. Cast Stone

W. 376; Fleischer v. Pelton Steel

§ 2] WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS 

2 the natural persons who procured its creation, the primary purposes of which are, on the part of the organizers, to procure, and, on the part of the state, to grant, limited liability in respect of obligations and a continuing existence independently of changes in membership or human mortality. For many purposes, as hereinafter shown, it is a "person" within the meaning of statutory provisions. Clearly, however, it is merely an artificial or fictitious person, having no existence except by law, without natural or moral qualities, and incapable of action, character, or conduct in and of itself.4 

Only through the agency of natural persons, its members and officers, can it contract and be contracted with, sue and be sued, manage its business, perform its functions, exercise its franchises, and accomplish the specific objects of its organization."

Except as authorized by law, no corporation can exist. 

And, though its existence is duly authorized, it is a mere creature of the act creating it, existing only by grace thereof, and in all its actions limited and governed by law.6 

§ 2. History. The theory of a corporation, or of an artificial entity endowed with certain powers, is of ancient origin. Under the Roman law, corporations were created by imperial or senatorial decree, with privileges 

104; McKnight v. President and

Trustees of the Town of Mineral 

Point, 1 Pin. 99. 

See, however, the interesting discussion by H. S. Richards, 

3 Wisconsin Law Rev. 130-132, as to the nature of a "corporation," whether wholly a fiction or creature of the law, or an association or composite of individuals.

[§ 3 and franchises limited and well defined, but amenable to the laws and cautiously and constantly watched against abuse of power or privileges. While the Roman ideas do not appear to have influenced development of our corporation law, the same theory was early recognized in England in the growth of municipal, charitable and ecclesiastical corporations, craft guilds and foreign trading corporations. By the end of the seventeenth century, several acts of parliament had been adopted authorizing the king to grant charters to various business associations. The practice then, and for many years afterward, both in this country and in England, was to create corporations only by special charters conferring valuable and exclusive franchises; and it was considered that, as the franchises were granted by the state, they could be vacated or forfeited only in a proceeding by the state. 

Now, however, corporations are formed under general laws, with the privilege of incorporation conferred upon all who comply with statutory conditions, and the state has no peculiar interest in the matter." § 3. § 5] 

WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS § 5. Distinctions and Advantages. A corporation is distinguishable from a partnership in that the members of the corporation, as natural persons, are merged into the corporate entity.25 Joint stock companies and associations are nothing more than partnerships, the members thereof being liable for debts of the company or association save as statutes may expressly provide to the contrary or give corporate attributes in certain particulars.26 Our supreme court has said, however, that a trading corporation may be likened in some respects to a partnership, in that the remedies of stockholders are much the same as those of partners.27

As a practical matter, the advantages of a corporation over a partnership lie in (1) avoiding personal liability of members on contracts and indebtedness of the company; (2) substituting majority control with power delegated to elected representatives for the power of any partner in a partnership to bind the firm by his acts within the scope of the firm business; and (3) preventing dissolution by death or bankruptcy of a member, or sale of a member's interest. Incorporation gives a continuity of existence uninterrupted by death or change of membership, limits liability of the members engaged in a hazardous or uncertain enterprise, permits large numbers of small investors to operate together, and gives to each a readily transferable interest.28

At one time, during the period of less lenient corporation laws in many of the states, "Massachusetts Trusts" flourished in some localities, and this form was adopted by some organizations, such as the large express companies, doing business in many states with widely divergent laws. The theory was to place property in the hands of trustees, contributors to the property or com-

Separate Entity. As hereinbefore stated, a corporation is a creature of statute and an artificial being.30 

The corporate entity is therefore distinct from that of its individual stockholders, officers and directors, though it can act only through the human agency of the latter.82 

Similarly, in the absence of fraud or unfairness, various corporations are none the less distinct because they have common officers, occupy common offices, and to a certain extent transact business for each other, and the fact of close alliance and practical identity of personnel does not prevent valid transaction of business between such corporations. Franchises. Every regularly organized corporation has a "franchise" to do business as a corporation.

§ 11. Court Control. The power of courts, on proper application, to prevent abuses in corporate management, is very broad.74 

Lyon, J., states in one of the earlier cases: "The visitorial or superintending power of the state over corporations created by the legislature will always be exercised, in proper cases, through the medium of the courts of the state, to keep those corporations within the limits of their lawful powers, and to correct and punish abuses of their franchises. To this end the courts will issue writs of quo warranto, mandamus or injunction, as the exigencies of the particular case may require; will inquire into the grievance complained of, and, if the same is found to exist, will apply such remedy as the law prescribes. Every corporation of the state, whether public or private, civil or municipal, is subject to this superintending control, although in its exercise different rules may be applied to different classes of corporations."' 75

[§ 12 Courts of equity may, accordingly, exercise supervisory control over corporations when they are (1) abusing powers given for public purposes, (2) committing breaches of trust, or (3) acting adversely to public policy. The courts, however, are cautious and very reluctant to interfere with the management or supervision of ordinary corporation affairs." They will not interfere with matters of business policy or of administration at the suit of minority stockholders and against the wishes of a majority of the directors and stockholders, in the absence of fraud and as long as the corporation is acting within the scope of its powers, regardless of the fact that the majority policy is unproductive or unwise.78

Under many circumstances the courts have jurisdiction, on grounds of public policy, to prevent a corporation from acting contrary to the intent for which it was created. The question of keeping a corporation acting within its powers is now regarded, as a general proposition, as one in which the state only is concerned; and ordinarily, therefore, the public must be represented in such an action, usually by intervention of the attorney general." But it appears that in case of an actual private wrong to some individual, as distinct from the public, occurring from a corporation exceeding its legal powers, a court of equity may act upon application of such private person to restrain the excesses.80

A "municipal" corporation is of the kind mentioned in article XI of the State Constitution-that is to say, a body corporate consisting of the inhabitants of a designated area, created by the legislature, with or without the consent of the inhabitants, for governmental purposes, possessing local legislative and administrative power, also power to exercise within its area so much of the administrative power of the state as may be delegated to it, and possessing limited capacity to own and hold property and to act in the purveyance of public conveniences.86

§ 14. In General. A corporation, being only an artificial creation of statute,¹ can exist only by authority and sanction of law. The right to form a corporation is statutory, and prior to organization a corporation has no being, franchises, or faculties.*

In earlier times, corporations were formed by special enactment or grant of a charter by the legislature; later, 1 See § 1, supra.

[§ by cumbersome procedure under general laws. But the formation of a corporation is now in its nature contractual, and is accomplished merely by filing a declaration of intent to be a corporation under a general law, or by a contractual obligation made with reference to a general law. For the formation of an ordinary business corporation, the steps are exceedingly simple, requiring only the procural by three or more competent organizers of a standard form of articles of organization from the office of the secretary of state, which they execute in duplicate as indicated thereon and return to the secretary of state with the statutory fee, whereupon the secretary of state returns the copy, which becomes in essence the "charter" of the corporation, for recording with the register of deeds of the county in which the corporation is to have its principal place of business,10 and upon due recording of the copy issues a certificate of incorporation. The corporation is then duly organized as such, though restricted from doing business with others than its own members until prescribed proportions of its capital stock have been subscribed and paid in.¹¹ 

The statutes also provide for abandonment of organization proceedings which have been begun, at any time before fifty per cent of the stock has been subscribed and twenty per cent paid in.¹º

§ 15. Statutes. The existence of a valid law under which a particular corporation might have been formed is essential to its existence even "de facto." 18 This proposition is now, however, but little likely to arise, as most corporations are organized under the general law, which permits incorporation for any lawful business or purpose whatever, and is thus so broad as to authorize the organization of practically any kind of corporation.¹4 

Certain types of corporations, such as railroad companies, insurance companies, and the like, are authorized by, and to be organized under, special statutes. A special law of this nature authorizing incorporation of a certain type of corporation will not be regarded as repealed by implication because a subsequent statute authorizes incorporation of companies along the same lines but with slightly broader powers.15 

There is said to be no doubt but that a private corporation may be created by the concurrent act of two or more states.18

Liability of promoters in these regards, however, is predicated on fraud, one essential element of which is deceit, and if an entire transaction is fully disclosed there is no deceit and can be no liability. The rule is not, therefore, that a promoter may not profit, but that he may not profit secretly and through want of good faith.86 

A promoter, who becomes an officer of the corporation, and as such, acting in conspiracy with other promoters, pays them an exorbitant price for property which will net the conspirators a secret profit, may be liable upon his bond for the money so paid.37 

§ 19. Sales to Corporation. The doctrine that promoters and organizers are duty-bound to make full and fair disclosure of facts within their knowledge to the corporation, and will not be permitted secretly to profit at its expense, finds particular application in cases where promoters attempt to "unload" property upon the corporation.38 If they intend to sell something to the corporation, they should, in fairness, provide it with a board of directors who will meet them at arm's length in dealing for it.39 Thus where promoters tell subscribers that the corporation will be permitted to purchase property at a particular figure, and that, by subscribing to the stock, they will be "in on the ground floor," but the promoters intend to, and do, sell the property to the corporation at a large profit per acre, there is no fair disclosure and the secret-profit doctrine applies.40 The same is true

Various means and subterfuges have been adopted to avoid the rule that secret profits belong to the corporation. It cannot be avoided by limiting membership in the corporation to persons interested in profiting from it until the transaction is completed and then selling stock to outsiders kept in ignorance of the true nature of the transaction, for those later innocently coming in may overturn the transaction or compel an accounting of the profits. § 22. Purpose of Organization. 

now be formed "for any lawful business or purpose whatever" under the provisions of the general corporation law, except as particular corporations, such as those to engage in banking, insurance, building or operating railroads, etc., are governed by special statutes.67 

Formerly the statutes enumerated various purposes or businesses which a corporation might be organized to engage in, adding the words "or for any lawful business purpose," and under this provision it was held that a corporation could legally be formed under the general law only for the primary business of engaging in some of the enterprises enumerated, or others similar thereto.68 But it was held that a telephone company might lawfully be formed under a provision for formation of telegraph companies "or any other lawful business or purpose whatever.", 69 As the statute now stands, there appears to be very little, if any, limitation upon the purpose of the corporation, except that it be "lawful." § 23. Name. The name chosen for a corporation must not contain the names of individuals in the manner in which they are ordinarily used in partnership or business names, and must distinguish the corporation from any other domestic corporation or corporation licensed to do business in the state. There can be but one authorized name,"¹ and it should be sufficiently different from that of any other corporation authorized to do business in the state so that the public will not be misled.72 The exclusive right of a corporation to its particular name was upheld, even at common law; but whether on special grounds, or as a trade-mark or trade name is not clear.78

The fact that one of the organizers has a name of commercial value and which he desires to use in the corporate name does not authorize its use in such manner as to cause confusion, and use thereof will be hedged with such limitations as are necessary to prevent unfair competition with a corporation previously in existence.74

§ 24. Articles of Organization. The making up and filing of proper articles of organization is one of the most important steps in organizing a corporation. The contents of these articles is prescribed by statute," and adequate forms therefor may be obtained from the secretary of state, except in the case of special or unusual corporations. Since, however, these articles become in effect the charter of the corporation, they are more particularly discussed in a subsequent chapter.78 

§ 25. Commencement of Business. While a corpora tion is duly organized when its articles of organization have been filed with the secretary of state with the requisite fee and a duplicate thereof recorded with the register of deeds of the county in which the principal place of business is located, it is forbidden to do business with others than its members until one-half of its stock has been subscribed and one-fifth thereof actually paid in, under penalty of having no right of action in respect of business done and personal liability on existing stockholders." Until the required percentage of stock is subscribed and paid in, it has been said that the corporation can have no legal meetings, or elect any officers, and its affairs can only be legally directed by the signers of the articles of incorporation.80 It is a corporation only in representative of the other, and the subject of similarity of name is extensively discussed).

§ 32. Charter-In General. The charter of a corpora tion, whether obtained under a general law or by special act of the legislature, is à legislative grant,¹ consisting of two parts: first, the right to be or exist as a corporation; and second, the right to do certain things in the exercise of powers conferred upon it by the state; and is the organic law of the corporation. As such, it is inherently unassignable, being a grant of special privileges to the corporators which enables them to act for certain designated purposes as a single individual and exempts them (unless otherwise specially provided) from individual

[§ 5 liability. In view of the decision of the Supreme Court of the United States, in the celebrated Dartmouth College Case, a corporate charter must likewise be regarded as a contract between the corporation and the state; but it stands on a different footing than a contract between private persons 7 and, in Wisconsin, is not within the impairment of contract clause of the Constitution because of a general reservation of power in the Constitution itself to alter or change corporate charters.³ 

Unless a special charter is shown, it will be presumed that a corporation which might have been organized under the general law was so organized.⁹ 

Formerly corporations were commonly formed by the enactment of a special "charter" by the legislature. In modern practice, however, practically all corporations are formed under general laws, and the charter actually consists of the filed and recorded articles of organization and the terms of the general law under which the corporation is formed.10

The "charter" is often spoken of as the corporate "franchise," but, as hereinbefore shown, is entirely distinct from and not to be confused with other franchises which the corporation may come to possess, such as those to build dams, occupy the streets of a city, and the like, these latter not being corporate adjuncts but licenses or special privileges which might equally have been

§ 33. 

-Contents. The contents of the articles of organization, which become the charter of the corporation, are prescribed by statute.12 They may properly fix the term of office of officers and directors, and it has been held that the term so fixed need not be limited to one year merely because the statutes provide for an annual election of directors.18 Although the statute provides that they shall state the "location" of the corporation, this does not permit the corporation, by naming a "principal place of business" in its articles, to fix its location for purposes of taxation, and such a designation is not binding on the taxing authorities.14 There is no authority for naming in the articles those who shall act as officers of the corporation,15 but the principal duties of the several · general officers must be stated, and it is not sufficient in this regard merely to recite that they shall have such duties as are imposed by law or by the board of directors.16

§ 34. 

-Statement of Purposes or Objects. The ob ject clause is the most important part of the charter. 

As pointed out by Louis S. Berkhoff, in an interesting study of the charter of the United States Steel Corporation, appearing in the Wisconsin Law Review,20 there has been much discussion as to the relative merits of long as against short object clauses. The danger of the long clause, of course, is that it may cause disastrous invocation of the settled doctrine of construction that expression of one thing by implication excludes others. But, on the other hand, the law as to implied powers of a corporation is not settled in all respects or in all jurisdictions; therefore, to make certain of powers desired, the long and carefully drawn object clause, claiming all powers as to which there might be any doubt and which might prove convenient, is probably still the safer practice. Thus, as the author of the article above referred to points out, it is well to include such matters, not readily or invariably implied, as a provision for lending to, guaranteeing or aiding projects of others. For the same reason, though power to hold stock in other corporations is clearly given by statute, it is safe practice to provide for its acquisition "by purchase, subscription, or otherwise," as a distinction has sometimes been made between power to purchase and power to subscribe, and also to provide for ownership "for investment, or other use, or otherwise make the provision broad enough to authorize ownership of a controlling interest. 99 In some states, in view of use of singular words in statutes relating to formation of corporations, it is held that a corporation organized thereunder can have but one 91.

It appears clear, however, from the language of the Wisconsin general incorporation law, that there is no such limitation in this state, and that a corporation may have as many objects or purposes as it desires, provided they are within the general law and do not bring it under some statute relating to banks, insurance companies, or the like.21

Professor Ballantine, in his recent work on Private Corporations, suggests, as particularly valuable, ancillary clauses with respect to carrying on various other businesses which it might possibly be desirable to engage in, giving full freedom of expansion; a clause empowering the company to enter into a joint venture or agreement for sharing profits or a partnership; a provision for promotion of other companies for purposes deemed beneficial; and one for guaranteeing contracts of customers and others.22

§ 36. 

-Force and Effect. It is obvious that provisions in articles of incorporation conflicting with statutes are void; that it is not within the power of the organizers of a corporation to nullify legislation." Lawful provisions, however, become the organic law of the corporation and are binding upon it. The fact that a particular provision is disregarded may amount to a waiver thereof in certain instances, but cannot eliminate it from the charter or take away its force in instances where it is not waived, as otherwise no one could tell what provisions of a charter were in force and it might be annulled or amended merely by disregard of its provisions.28

§ 38. Subsequent Legislation. A by-law is a permanent and continuing rule for the government of the corporation and its officers, and the purpose of by-laws is to regulate management of the corporate affairs so that it may more readily and conveniently fulfil the purposes for which it was created. They are, essentially, the laws of the corporations, and may be made either of general or of limited duration, according to necessity or convenience. § 42. 

-Adoption or Enactment. The power to enact or adopt by-laws resides primarily in the stockholders, and their right to make the by-laws is important." This power may, by charter provision or by action of the stockholders, be vested in the board of directors; but the directors have no power in this connection unless it is so given to them.75 By-laws may, however, be adopted, or deemed adopted, by acts or conduct of the corporation as well as by express vote or adoption in writing, unless it is otherwise provided." Accordingly, although power to adopt by-laws is vested in the directors by the articles of incorporation, such regulations will be deemed properly enacted, although actually adopted at a stockholders' meeting held prior to recording of the articles of incorporation, where they are thereafter treated by the directors as the by-laws of the corporation."

Even a chamber of commerce does not have unlimited power to pass by-laws, but is limited to the purposes of its creation and incorporation.81 But an executed contract made in good faith with a corporation will prevail over a by-law with which it may come in conflict, likewise over the organic act creating the corporation, if the contract is not clearly prohibited by statute or contrary to public policy.82

As long as a by-law, duly adopted, stands unrepealed, it is obviously binding upon the corporation and its members.88 Even though not formally enacted, or irregularly adopted, it may become binding by acquiescence, or an estoppel may arise preventing those who have acquiesced in it from challenging its validity. Strangers contracting with the corporation are not presumed to know its by-laws and are not ordinarily bound thereby. Courts are reluctant to invalidate a contract, for example, as against a third person dealing with the corporation, because of by-laws restricting authority of the officer who acted for the corporation or imposing formalities upon contracting for the corporation.85 But where a by-law expressly gives certain rights to third persons upon complying with the conditions thereof, one who acts in reliance upon the by-law and complies with its terms is entitled to have it enforced for his benefit.8 86 prohibiting transfer of stock without consent of all stockholders.

§ 44. 

Violations. Violations of the by-laws of a corporation may be heard before and punished by a tribunal created by the by-laws themselves, and courts will not interfere with the functioning of such a board upon the mere assertion that it will act in excess of its powers. 87

§ 45. 

Construction and Pleading. If a by-law is unambiguous, its construction is a question of law for the court; if ambiguous, but capable of explanation by extrinsic evidence, its construction is usually a question of fact for the jury. But by-laws are not to be construed with the strictness of acts of the legislature, but rather like contracts between individuals. If no question is made as to reasonableness, or that the by-law is against law or contrary to public policy, ambiguities may be resolved in the light of the practical interpretation put upon them by the parties or by the members of the corporation.91

§ 46. Changes and Amendments. Except as to by-laws of a contractural nature, the law is liberal as to power of a corporation to amend or repeal its by-laws, or to suspend their operation in emergency. The fact that the by-laws are referred to as the "constitution" of the corporation does not make them unalterable.95 But where a by-law provides that the funds of the corporation are to be used only in a specified manner, and that this manner can be altered only by certain definite procedure, such provisions amount to a contract and can be altered only as therein provided.96

Determination of what is within the scope of the corporate powers is, however, ordinarily an administrative question, to be decided primarily by the governing authority of the corporation. As hereinafter shown, it is rare that anyone save the state can question the power of a corporation in respect of an act not in itself unlawful.® 

The present Wisconsin general corporation law is broad in its provisions, conferring ample power upon corporations for the accomplishment of all legitimate purposes of their formation." The powers thus conferred have been incorporated into special charters by general provision that corporations organized under such charters shall "have and possess all the powers and privileges and be subject to all the duties" prescribed by the general corporation laws "and shall also have all peculiar rights and privileges granted to them respectively by their charters or any special law not inconsistent with these statutes." 8 by Louis S. § 48. Legislative Control. The legislature may con fer such powers upon corporations as it deems proper,⁹ and may also limit or restrict powers previously conferred.10 The general prohibition of the State Constitution against grant of corporate powers other than by general law does not preclude grant of such powers by special law in furtherance of the police power of the state and in aid of public health."1

§ 54. Holding Stock in Other Corporations. Under the common law a corporation has no power to subscribe for or purchase and hold stock in another corporation, unless clearly authorized by statute or by its charter.44 

But in Wisconsin such power is expressly given to corporations organized under the general law. This power was formerly limited to cases where three-fourths of the stock in both corporations assented at a general or special meeting, and it was held that an executory agreement to purchase stock in another corporation was void unless such assent was given at a regular or special meeting of the stockholders,46 and intimated that officers and directors were thereby deprived of power, without the assent of the stockholders, to transfer practically the entire business plant of the corporation for stock in another corporation.* 47 Whether ownership of stock in other corporations is confined to those having like purposes is more or less of an open question. The weight of authority elsewhere appears to be the effect that the power is so limited, save where stock in another corporation is acquired in the ordinary course of the business of the purchasing corporation, as where taken for a debt due it, or the like.48

§ 55. Acts Ultra Vires or in Excess of Powers-In 

General. Although many inroads have been made of late years upon the doctrine, it may still be stated generally that a corporation cannot legally bind itself or be bound by acts in excess of its powers, express and implied, and foreign to the purposes of its organization.50 and acts so attempted are designated in law as "ultra vires" acts.51 

This rule was formerly strict, and it is stated, for example in one of the early opinions, that "a moment's consideration of the great increase of corporations in modern times, and of the vast powers entrusted to them, as well as of the natural tendency of their accumulated capital to accumulate also influence and power, is sufficient to satisfy every intelligent mind of the absolute necessity of adhering to the rule confining these bodies strictly to the accomplishment of those ends and objects which their charters authorize, and prohibiting them from all others." 52 It was also said that an express prohibition in a charter against the doing of some particular act was of but little effect, as, in the absence of any provision authorizing the corporation to do the act, the rule that it could do only those things authorized by its charter would apply.58

The early rule, accordingly, was that a corporation could do only those things which were expressly authorized or were "necessary" to the accomplishment of the corporate purpose; 54 that charters were to be construed strictly, and contracts not within the powers given as so construed were void and not even capable of ratification.55 

But, as hereinabove shown in discussing the implied powers of corporations, these views have long since been modified, and the present tendency is to regard a corporation as having power by implication to do anything convenient or adapted to its business which an individual might do, in the absence of express prohibitions.56 The doctrine of ultra vires, under the modern trend of decisions, has lost its importance and, in fact, almost disappeared.57 Contracts entered into by a corporation in excess of its powers are at most illegal, not void; 58 and on breach of the contract by the opposite party the corporation is at least entitled to recover advances made, unless the agreement was against public policy or some positive prohibition.59

Acts wherein power exists but is irregularly exercised are, of course, to be distinguished from those which are ultra vires or beyond the power of the corporation no matter how done; and in some instances it appears that 60

§ 56. -Right to Challenge Validity Generally. § 60. Power to Acquire and Hold Property. Ever since the enactment of the ancient English statutes of "mortmain," the power of corporations to take and hold real estate has been the subject of great concern and jealousy. But it is not the aim of the law to hamper the doing of legitimate business by corporations.¹ Wisconsin corporations organized under the general law are expressly empowered to take and hold property, both real and personal, including stock in other corporations, 1 Farmers' & Millers' Bank v. 

Detroit & M. R. Co., 17 Wis. 372.

[§ and to acquire rights, privileges or franchises granted to any person by the state which would directly aid the business of the corporation. Certain corporations are also given rights of eminent domain to condemn property for their needs, or authorized to acquire such lands as may be necessary for ponds and reservoirs." It is well settled, furthermore, that a corporation facing a prospective loss in the course of its ordinary business may take a real estate mortgage or buy in property to protect itself," and that a corporation authorized to sell or deal on credit may take proper security, including real estate mortgages, for the payment of obligations due it, or the payment of subscriptions to its stock. All property lawfully held by a corporation is within the protection of constitutional provisions against deprivation without due process of law, and the like, the same as property of an individual.⁹

Whenever it is competent for a corporation lawfully to acquire and hold property of the particular kind, the presumption of innocence applies and it is presumed, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that property of that kind was lawfully acquired and is so held.¹º A stranger claiming the property adversely to the corporation cannot set up want of power in the corporation to hold such property, unless the corporation is expressly prohibited from holding it." § 65. -Transfers to Officers and Members. § 66.

§ 68. Rights of Stockholders. The legal title to cor porate property is in the corporation, not the stockholders, the corporation being a distinct legal entity.59 

This is true even though a single individual buys up all the stock; and a sole stockholder is not for that reason entitled to maintain a possessory action in respect of property of the corporation. Nevertheless, the property, subject to debts and the rights of creditors,61 equitably belongs to the members or stockholders,62 and they are entitled to whatever remains after the corporation has ceased to function as such and exhausted its purposes, and the debts have been paid. In this respect the rights of the stockholders are like those of partners,64 or the corporation may be regarded as a trustee for management of the property and the stockholders as the cestuis que trustent.65

For a time it was quite generally accepted, but has since been repudiated in most states and never found a firm foothold in Wisconsin.67 Accordingly, in Wisconsin, creditors have no standing to complain of a transfer by the corporation to a stockholder of some of its property in payment of a debt due the stockholder, the remaining property at that time and at a fair valuation considerably exceeding its remaining liabilities. The same is true even of transfers to directors or officers who are bona fide creditors, as long as the corporation is solvent and a going concern.

A solvent corporation having no actual intent to defraud creditors may dispose of its property for an inadequate consideration or by voluntary conveyance, the same as an individual, and neither existing nor subsequent creditors can question the transaction, though the corporation subsequently becomes insolvent.70

§ 71] WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS § 71. -Fraudulent Transfers. Transfers made by a corporation with actual intent to hinder, delay and defraud its creditors, or some of them, are open to attack by other creditors, to the same extent as like transfers by individuals.76 But a creditor seeking to attack such a transfer must first reduce his claim to judgment, the same as when attacking such a transfer made by an individual debtor." Any creditor appearing in the action to have the transfer set aside is bound by the decree, though he does not actually litigate his claim or demand against the corporation.78

A transfer is in fraud of creditors and subject to being set aside at suit of either past or future creditors where the corporation purports to transfer property, rendering itself insolvent, to one of its stockholders, in consideration of his surrender of his stock, but the corporation thereafter continues to do business with the property apparently as its own.79 The transaction is likewise open. to attack where a corporation, grossly and obviously insolvent, voluntarily places all its property in an express trust for the benefit of only a part of its creditors.80 It appears, moreover, that the directors may themselves be held liable to creditors where, the corporation being largely indebted, they transfer all its property without consideration to another corporation and permit one of their number to withdraw and convert assets to a large amount.81

§ 72. Contracts Generally. All stock corporations, when not expressly or by implication forbidden to do so, have general power to make contracts furthering the objects of their creation. This authority exists by necessary inference from the general power conferred on the corporation to do business.¹ Domestic corporations are also, by statute, expressly given power to make contracts necessary and proper to affect their purposes and conduct their business.

§ 73] WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS 

§ 73. Validity of Contracts-In General. A contract of a corporation which is of a nature expressly prohibited by statute is void. While some of the early cases also declared to be void contracts which were beyond the powers of the corporation as conferred by law and its charter, this rule no longer obtains with its former strictness, and the defense that a contract was ultra vires, as hereinbefore shown, is now rarely available, either to the corporation or to one who contracts with it. Want of power to enter into the particular transaction, in the absence of express prohibition, is now a matter which can, in general, be raised only by the state, or by a stockholder who has not assented to the deal and acts promptly to have it enjoined or nullified before it has been performed on either side. It is a mistake to assume that a mere statutory regulation of the manner of making a corporate contract is a prohibitory law, rendering void a transaction executed in good faith for disregard of its provisions. Under the modern view, an executed contract made in good faith prevails over a bylaw with which it comes in conflict, or even over the organic act creating the corporation, if the contract is not clearly prohibited by statute or contrary to public policy. Obviously, therefore, the fact that parts of a

Any contract of a corporation which is against public policy is, of course, unenforceable, as in the case of contracts of individuals. The courts will not lend their aid to the enforcement of such transactions. 

A scheme to raise money by selling "certificate contracts," each purporting to be a contract to convey an undivided one acre out of a tract containing a specified number of acres in Honduras, and containing no means of identifying the tract, has been branded as fraudulent upon its face.⁹ 

But a contract is not void merely because it is part of an organized plan of the corporation to issue obligations against expectant profits and the plan is highly speculative from the point of view of the obligee.10 While, ordinarily, the corporate management must be impartial as among stockholders, this does not prevent a corporation from validly lending its credit and assets to one faction of stockholders, to enable them to buy out the others, where the various factions are at war to the detriment of the corporation.11

A corporation is prohibited by statute from transacting business with others than its members until one-half of its stock has been subscribed and one-fifth paid in.12 

In view of this express prohibition, it cannot validly contract with nonmembers until the required percentage has been subscribed and paid; 18 and the members are personally liable if it does.14

Although corporations have almost identical officers and members, they are still separate entities and may validly transact business each with the other.15

§ 73] WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS § 73. Validity of Contracts-In General. A contract of a corporation which is of a nature expressly prohibited by statute is void. While some of the early cases also declared to be void contracts which were beyond the powers of the corporation as conferred by law and its charter, this rule no longer obtains with its former strictness, and the defense that a contract was ultra vires, as hereinbefore shown, is now rarely available, either to the corporation or to one who contracts with it. Want of power to enter into the particular transaction, in the absence of express prohibition, is now a matter which can, in general, be raised only by the state, or by a stockholder who has not assented to the deal and acts promptly to have it enjoined or nullified before it has been performed on either side. It is a mistake to assume that a mere statutory regulation of the manner of making a corporate contract is a prohibitory law, rendering void a transaction executed in good faith for disregard of its provisions. Under the modern view, an executed contract made in good faith prevails over a bylaw with which it comes in conflict, or even over the organic act creating the corporation, if the contract is not clearly prohibited by statute or contrary to public policy. Obviously, therefore, the fact that parts of a

Any contract of a corporation which is against public policy is, of course, unenforceable, as in the case of contracts of individuals. The courts will not lend their aid to the enforcement of such transactions. 

A scheme to raise money by selling "certificate contracts,” each purporting to be a contract to convey an undivided one acre out of a tract containing a specified number of acres in Honduras, and containing no means of identifying the tract, has been branded as fraudulent upon its face.⁹ 

But a contract is not void merely because it is part of an organized plan of the corporation to issue obligations against expectant profits and the plan is highly speculative from the point of view of the obligee.10 While, ordinarily, the corporate management must be impartial as among stockholders, this does not prevent a corporation from validly lending its credit and assets to one faction of stockholders, to enable them to buy out the others, where the various factions are at war to the detriment of the corporation.¹¹

A corporation is prohibited by statute from transacting business with others than its members until one-half of its stock has been subscribed and one-fifth paid in.¹2

In view of this express prohibition, it cannot validly contract with nonmembers until the required percentage has been subscribed and paid; 18 and the members are personally liable if it does.14

Although corporations have almost identical officers and members, they are still separate entities and may validly transact business each with the other.15

WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS § 74. -Contracts or Agreements in Restraint of 

Trade. It is not within the scope of this work to go extensively into monopolies and agreements in restraint of trade, the law in this regard not being in any way peculiar to corporations. It is sufficient in this regard to note that combinations in restraint of trade were il legal at common law,16 and, as a general proposition, are prohibited both by federal and state "anti-trust" legislation." Of recent years, however, the tendency has been away from regarding monopolies as unmitigated evils, particularly as to farm marketing and co-operative ventures, and labor organizations, 18 and it is clearly within the power of the legislature to make reasonable classifications in this connection, exempting upon economic grounds monopolistic agreements of the classes mentioned from operation of the anti-trust laws.19

§ 76. Corporation as Bound by Contract-In General. 

As a general proposition, a corporation can contract only through its board of directors or by their authority,29 and action of the board is to be shown by its records.30 

There are so many exceptions to this rule, however, that it is of little practical use; for it is well settled that a corporation may be bound by custom, by acquiescence, and in other ways without formal action of the directors.1 Thus it may be bound by estoppel or ratification where it accepts the benefits of acts done on its hehalf.82

§ 78. -Promoters' Contracts. The subject of power of the promoters and organizers of a corporation to bind it by their acts is treated in a preceding chapter.42 There can be no question of the power of a corporation, after it comes into existence, to adopt such contracts, if within the scope of the corporate powers, and to enjoy the benefits or subject itself to liabilities thereunder.48 Whether there is an adoption or ratification of a transaction entered into by the promoters or organizers depends upon circumstances.44 The fact that an agreement similar to that which the promoters had arranged is entered into by the corporation is not conclusive, if the terms are different and it is in fact a new deal.45 

After articles of incorporation have been duly filed and recorded, and prior to election of officers and directors, the signers of the articles of incorporation are by law authorized to manage the affairs of the corporation.46 

During this period, therefore, no ratification or adoption is necessary to make contracts made by them on behalf of the corporation binding upon it, for they are the actual management of the corporation, empowered to act for it.47

[§ $79. Corporation as Entitled to Benefits of Contract. 

An error in the name of a corporation in a contract or writing does not prevent enforcement of the contract by or on behalf of the corporation.48 Similarly, although an officer of the corporation in signing a contract omits to add his official designation, the corporation, having performed the contract on its part and adopted it as its own, may maintain suit in its own name thereon.49 In fact, although a corporation is not named at all in a written contract or memorandum thereof, it may nevertheless show that it was an undisclosed principal or that the contract was made on its behalf or for its benefit, and thus enforce performance or seek damages for breach of the contract.50 No preliminary reformation of the instru ment is necessary to a recovery thereon, upon a showing that by mistake it was made in the name of the directors or officers personally.51

Those who have accepted and retain large benefits under a contract with a corporation are estopped to deny that it was not formally authorized by the directors.52

§ 82. -Consideration for Issuance. The statutes forbid issuance by a corporation of "any bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, except for money or for labor or property estimated at its true money value, actually received by it, equal to seventy-five per cent of the par value thereof," and further provide that bonds issued contrary to this prohibition "shall be void." 72 These provisions have become part of the public policy of the state,78 and the courts do not hesitate to give them full force and effect." The object is to protect stockholders and bona fide creditors against the improvident issuing of bonds. A corporation accordingly cannot validly pledge its bonds for a loan of less than seventy-five per cent of par value.76 Issuance of bonds for an antecedent debt has been held not issuance for money, labor or property, and the bonds not enforceable unless in the hands of a bona fide holder." But where, on a pledge of bonds, there is an agreement, express or implied, that the pledgee will account for the bonds at not less than the statutory percentage, the arrangement is valid.78

§ 84. Civil Liability for Torts or Wrongs-In General. 

As a general proposition, whether a corporation is liable for a tort or wrong is to be determined upon the same principles as in the case of an individual.88 It is well settled that a corporation, like a private individual, is liable for the torts of its agents when acting within the scope of their employment and in furtherance of the corporate business,89 notwithstanding the means used were not authorized and there was no reasonable ground to expect that they would be used.90 A corporation may thus become liable for malicious prosecution or false imprison-

§ 91. "Capital" Distinguished. Though the "capi tal" and the "capital stock" of a corporation are frequently confused, and the terms sometimes carelessly used as synonymous, there is a fundamental difference which should be observed. Kinds of Stock-Common Stock. The "com mon" stock of a corporation is the ordinary, nonpreferred share issued to a stockholder, giving the holder certain rights and privileges as to voting and dividends, but to which are attached no special privileges or guarantees on the part of the corporation. The holder of such stock is entitled to participate in the profits, if any, after all obligations are paid, and in such assets of the corporation as may remain upon dissolution after all obligations have been met, but his rights are subsidiary to those of holders of preferred stock to the extent of the preference given them.15 Even the common stock, moreover, is subject to classification, and there may thus be common stock with, and other common stock in the same corporation without, par value,16 or some with and some without voting power. § 93. Preferred Stock. Wisconsin corporations are authorized to issue preferred stock when it is so provided in their articles of incorporation or by an amendment thereto adopted by a three-fourths vote of the stock, and the preferred stock may be made cumulative, and preferred as to either or both profits and assets, and voting power denied or restricted.19 There may also be a second issue of such stock. But no change in relation to preferred stock once issued can be made except by amendment to the articles of incorporation adopted by vote of three-fourths of both the preferred and common stock.21 

Preferred stock cannot be issued without par value.22

Whether or not it is to the benefit of a corporation to issue preferred stock depends on circumstances. Such stock naturally appeals to the more timid class of investors, because of its preference rights. The holders are first to be paid out of profits, whether holders of common stock receive anything or not. On the other hand, the profits of holders of preferred stock are limited to

894.- Stock Without Par Value or "Nonpar"

Stock. Wisconsin corporations may also, where so authorized by the articles of incorporation or an amendment thereof, issue common stock without nominal or par value, which may be issued in various classes differing as to voting powers or restrictions, and sold for such consideration as shall be fixed by the directors, organizers or stockholders, as provided by statute.25

Most of the states which are at all advanced in legislation with respect to corporations now authorize issuance of such stock. The original theory in allowing it was the unfairness of requiring that stock bear a fixed par value where its actual value must, of necessity, continually fluctuate with the success of the business of the corporation; further, that the existence of par stock had a tendency to mislead the public and creditors into relying on authorized capital stock or stated par value rather than

There is also a danger of fraud on subscribers and investors, when nonpar stock is used, by dilution of the stock already issued by subsequent issues at lower prices, or of watering a future issue by an original issue without consideration, where the law permits each issue to be made at such price as may be fixed, irrespective of the price for prior or subsequent issues.28 The blessings of nonpar stock provisions are therefore, as in the case of most "progressive legislation," not entirely unmixed. There is, however, a great and noteworthy trend towards its use by the larger corporations, particularly those whose stock is dealt in upon the open market.29

§ 97. -Compelling Issuance. One who owns stock in a corporation is entitled to have a certificate evidencing his rights.48 If the proper directors or officers improperly refuse to issue a certificate, they may be compelled by court action to do so. The theory of such an action, where plaintiff has become the owner by purchase from an existing stockholder, is not that specific perform- ´ance is sought against the corporation, but that its officers, as trustees, must perform their duty.45 

Loss or destruction of a stock certificate is not fatal to the rights of the owner. If the corporation refuses to issue a new certificate in its place, it may be compelled to do so by application to a court of competent jurisdiction and the giving of a sufficient bond.4

§ 98. -Form and Contents. No particular form is prescribed for certificates of stock, except that, if there is both preferred and common stock, the "certificates of preferred stock and common stock shall state, on the face thereof, or on the reverse side with an appropriate reference thereto on the face thereof, all privileges accorded to and all restrictions imposed on preferred stock," and if the corporation is to have any lien or rights restricting transfer, such right or lien must be stated on the certificate or it is not effective.48 Standard forms are obtainable from almost any large printer or stationer. 

Stock certificates are usually signed by the president and countersigned by the secretary and sealed with the seal of the corporation.49 But the secretary has no authority to issue a certificate as "fully paid” where only a portion of the subscription has been paid.50 

§ 99.

Christian name in a stock certificate may, it has been held, be shown either by parol evidence or from other documents.52

§ 101. Blue Sky Laws. The "Securities Law," better known as the "Blue Sky Law," relates to all manner of dealings in stocks, bonds and securities. Its aim is not particularly to regulate corporations, but rather to protect the public against the machinations and schemes of high pressure promoters and security salesmen.62 The constitutionality, generally, of such legislation is beyond question. When other remedies to collect have been exhausted against the corporation without success, they may maintain a suit in the nature of a creditors' bill to enforce payment of unpaid subscriptions.29 Such an action is not, however, strictly a creditors' bill, because it involves no question of fraud, but only one of debt.80 While it has been said that the action is brought in the right of the corporation,³¹ defenses which would have been good as against the corporation are not always good as against the creditors-as, for example, a defense of the statute of limitations or failure to present a claim against the estate of a decedent.82 Any particular creditor or group of creditors pursuing this course can enforce the subscription liabilities only for the benefit of all the creditors of the corporation, not solely for himself or themselves.83

§ 110. -Fraud in Obtaining Subscriptions. As to whether there was fraud in inducing a person to subscribe for stock, the usual rules and principles as to what constitutes "fraud" control. The corporation is not responsible for misrepresentations made by a person who was neither its officer nor agent and whose acts have not been ratified or adopted, but is responsible for acts of an agent within the scope of his authority," and for ratified or adopted acts of a promoter.48 There is no liability for immaterial representations, though false, or mere statements of future intent which do not relate to existing fact.50 But representations need not have been knowingly false to be fraudulent, if simple and easily made tests would have shown the truth and their falsity should accordingly have been known.51

§ 112. 

-Meetings of Subscribers. Subscribers to stock in a corporation may hold meetings, if they see fit so to do, and may lay down such rules as they please as to voting privileges. But a creditor who merely agrees with a promoter to take stock in a reorganized corporation in payment of the debt due him is not a "subscriber' or entitled to notice of a preliminary meeting of subscribers to perfect organization.74 

§ 113. -Payment. Payment of the amount sub scribed toward the capital of a corporation is ordinarily made upon call or assessment, or the subscription may be to pay by fixed instalments.76 If payment is not made when due, it can be compelled by action." Where, by the subscription agreement, delivery of stock and payment therefor are to be contemporaneous, notice to the subscriber at maturity of a note given by him for his subscription, stating that the stock is ready, is sufficient to place him in default, although the stock is not then actually ready, if he makes no attempt to pay.78

Ordinarily, the taking of the subscriber's note for the amount due is not payment.79 Subscription liability is not extinguished as against creditors, moreover, by a purported distribution of entirely fictitious profits, crediting them upon payments due.80 But a subscription may be paid by crediting the subscriber with salary due him as an officer and advances made by him to the corporation, where the transaction is in entire good faith.³¹ After a corporation has made an assignment for the benefit of creditors, a subscriber may pay the assignee and will

§ 114. Issuance of Stock. Stock is ordinarily consid ered as "issued" by delivery of a stock certificate to the person entitled thereto.88 Such a certificate, however, is mere evidence of ownership and not in itself "stock" or a "share" of stock.84 When stock has been fully paid for, issuance of a certificate is accordingly not necessary to regarding the stock as "issued." 85 Issuance by officers of the corporation is ratified by maintenance of an action controlled by the directors to recover the agreed price of the stock.86

Legality of stock issued is determinable by an action to that end in equity.87 In such an action, brought by a stockholder to cancel stock alleged to have been illegally issued by the directors, the directors are proper but not necessary parties.88 As incidental relief, the right of a director to whom the stock was issued to hold office as such may be determined and the incumbent removed or enjoined from presuming further to exercise authority.89

Furthermore, property value may fluctuate from time to time. For this reason, it would be unfair to permit a corporation to take property at an agreed value, paying for it with stock, and later to assert that it was a bad bargain or that the property was not as valuable as was anticipated. The rule therefore is that a corporation, having issued stock purporting to be fully paid for property transferred to it, cannot thereafter assert that the stock was not fully paid and attempt to collect an alleged balance due.¹¹ But creditors, dealing with the corporation in ignorance of the situation, are not so bound. § 119. Cancellation of Fictitious or Watered

As hereinbefore explained, where stock is issued for property the situation is somewhat different from that where it is issued on a cash payment of less than par. 

The same principles apply, but due to the possibility of a bona fide disagreement as to the value of property, a stronger showing, and one amounting to a showing of actual fraud, must be made before even the creditors can demand that the difference between actual value of the property and par value of the stock be paid in.86 

§ 121. Rights and Liabilities of Holder of Watered Stock. By statute, par value stock issued for less than par is "void." 87 But it is subject to validation by payment of the balance due up to par, and apparently holders of such stock may exercise all rights of stockholders up to the time when their power to exercise such rights is legally challenged. Watered or fictitious stock is subject to challenge even in the hands of one who relied upon a statement on the face of the certificate that it was fully paid, and who purchased such certificate in good faith and for value, and no rights as stockholder are acquired by purchase of such a certificate. In such case, however, the purchaser may proceed against the corporation for damages as liable for the wrongful act of its officer in issuing a fully paid certificate.89

§ 122. Calls and Assessments-In General. A "call" 

is an official declaration by the directors that the sum subscribed, or a specified instalment thereof, is required to be paid. It is the method prescribed by statute for maturing stock subscriptions or calling in portions of the amount due, where not otherwise expressly provided by law, the articles of incorporation, or the subscription contract; 48 and a call is necessary and a condition precedent to enforcing liability in such cases. But if the subscription itself fixes definite instalments due at specified times, there is no necessity for a call.45 44 The power to make a call or assessment is wholly statutory, and in the absence of authority in the statutes, articles of incorporation, or by-laws, directors have no power to call or assess, or to subject stock to sale for nonpayment of a call or assessment.48 A stockholder, however, is none the less liable in fact for the balance due because there has been no call maturing his obligation.47

§ 124. -Time and Mode of Making Assessment. 

The statutes provide that calls and assessments are to be made by the directors, "in such proportion and at such times as they shall think proper, by giving such notice thereof as the by-laws shall prescribe."' 51 When to make an assessment is thus left up to the directors. One may be made before all capital is subscribed where the law under which the corporation is formed so provides; 52 but, in the absence of statute, no assessment can be made save for such first payment as is required by the subscription agreement until all authorized stock has been subscribed, and in view of the Wisconsin statute requiring that one-half the stock be subscribed and onefifth paid in before a corporation can do business with others than its members, no call can be made until such percentages have been subscribed and paid.58 Notice of the assessment is required,54 and is to be given "as the by-laws shall prescribe," thus making the existence of a duly enacted by-law as to notice a condition precedent.5

§ 125. Actions to Collect or Recover. If a call or assessment duly made is not paid, it may be enforced by suit in the name of the corporation. The complaint in such an action should, of course, set forth all matters necessary to show a regular and valid call and that the defendant has failed to pay.63 Any sum in which the corporation is indebted to the particular subscriber may be pleaded as an offset or counterclaim.64 

§ 126. 

Forfeiture of Stock for Nonpayment. The statutes provide that if any stockholder neglects or refuses payment for a specified time after a call becomes due and payable, and after he has been notified, his stock may be sold by the directors at public auction, upon thirty days' notice by publication, the stockholder to remain liable for any deficiency if such sale does not bring enough to pay the assessment and expenses of sale.65

§ 129. Rights of Existing Stockholders. It is thoroughly settled in Wisconsin that on an increase of capital existing stockholders are entitled to retain their relative and proportionate voice in the control and management of the corporation, and each must be given an opportunity to purchase an amount of the stock increase proportionate to his existing holdings before the new stock is offered for sale to outsiders.76 Existing stockholders, to protect their rights in this regard, need not hunt out the corporate officers and make an offer; it is up to the corporation to see that they have an opportunity to purchase, and such an opportunity is not given by merely offering the stock for sale to the highest bidder." 

The same principle applies where only part of the stock originally authorized was sold, and it is determined to issue the remainder,78 or where treasury stock bought in by the corporation is to be reissued.79 This right does not extend to compelling issuance of stock, but does attach at once when the stock is to be issued.80 The existing stockholders are entitled to the aid of a court of equity to protect their rights in this connection, if nec-

§ 134. -Warranties. On sale of a stock certificate, the seller, unless a contrary intent appears, is implied by law to warrant that the certificate is genuine, that he. has a legal right to transfer it, and that he has no knowledge of any fact which would impair the validity of the certificate. There may also, of course, be express warranties.

§ 136. -Agreements to Repurchase or Resell. Sales of stock are sometimes made with an option or agreement to resell or to repurchase.18 An option to repurchase is not without consideration where given as part of a transaction wherein the seller agrees to sell at a fixed price on consideration of cancellation of a debt due from him to the corporation.17 Such an option, made conditional upon the stock not being sold to another before its exercise, cannot be avoided by a merely colorable transfer of the stock to the husband or wife of the opposite party.18 Nor is the agreement void for uncertainty because of failure to specify the exact number of shares to be resold by each of several purchasers who purchased jointly, where the intention can be made clear by extrinsic evidence showing the facts and circumstances surrounding the transaction.19

§ 138. -Passing of Title. The usual mode of transferring stock, as between the parties, is by delivery of a stock certificate indorsed in blank or to the transferee.28 A blank indorsement, plus delivery of the certificate, is sufficient to pass title, though the charter or by-laws of the corporation and the certificate itself provide that shares shall be transferable only on the books of the corporation or require registration or transfer by a transfer agent.25 The Uniform Stock Transfer Act, however, also authorizes a transfer of title by delivery of the certificate and a separate document containing a written assignment or power of attorney, either in blank or to a specified person.28 Unless one of these methods is excellent discussion of the effect of this act may be found in an article by Clarence G. § 139. -On Books of Corporation. A transfer of stock as between individuals is one thing, its recognition by the corporation is another. As a general proposition, until stock is presented for transfer on the books of the corporation it need take no notice of a change of ownership or accord any rights to one claiming to be a transferee, and until the transfer is reflected by the corporate records there is no notice to third persons or to the public at large. 84 Once a transfer has been made on the corporate books, however, it is presumed to have been made in the usual course of business.35 

Transfer on the books of the corporation is merely a ministerial act on the part of the officer charged with the duty of making such transfers,86 and he has no power to try and determine controversies as to ownership 87 or consider the motives and intentions of the parties. The fact that a transfer is made is accord- 37 from taking title, if the transferee from whom he purchased was still in possession of the certificate. Stats. § 183.08.

§ 142. In General. A dividend is a division among the stockholders of a corporation of its surplus profits.' 

It is made pursuant to declaration or resolution of the management, usually for payment in cash, but may be for distribution in the form of additional stock, or possibly even in goods. It is no dividend, however, but a distribution of capital, for a corporation, purchasing the entire stock of another corporation with the proceeds of a loan obtained by the purchasing corporation, to distribute the purchased stock pro rata among its own stockholders.5 

§ 143. Declaration of Dividends. The power to de clare dividends is ordinarily in the board of directors."

It is for the directors to determine whether the status of the business is such as to make a dividend advisable," whether there are surplus profits from which a dividend can be paid, and, if there are such profits, the amount of them that should be distributed. In the absence of fraud or bad faith, there is no power to compel the directors to act,¹¹ and there is no right to recover a dividend until they have declared one.12

§ 148. Liability of Directors for Paying Unlawful 

Dividends. By statute, the directors of a corporation are made personally liable for paying dividends before fifty per cent of the stock has been paid in or when the corporation is insolvent or in danger of insolvency, "not having reason to believe that there were sufficient net profits properly applicable thereto to pay the same without impairing or diminishing the capital. The liability imposed is not alone for the amount paid out as dividends, but "to the creditors of the corporation at the time of declaring such dividends to the amount of their claim, "38 and is therefore penal in effect.84 It is immaterial on liability of a particular director whether he personally participated in declaration of the dividend, if he accepted his portion and thereby apparently sanctioned the distribution. 85 36 The statutory liability of the directors is, moreover, joint and several, and each director is thus individually liable to all creditors, as a class, who were such at the time the dividend was paid." § 149. Right to Receive Dividends-Life Tenant or 

Remainderman. Where stock is left in trust, for the benefit of one person for life, and, after his death, to another, dividends declared during the life of the life tenant, whether payable in cash or in stock, as a general proposition go to the life tenant unless the person creating the trust otherwise directed. He is ordinarily entitled to all such dividends, or parts of dividends, as are attributable to profits of the corporation earned since his interest came into being.40 But surplus merely accumulated by a corporation, and not declared as a dividend during the life of the life beneficiary does not belong to the life tenant, and his heirs have no right to dividends paid after his death, though out of profits accumulated during his life; such dividends go to the remainderman.41 In the absence of a clear expression to the contrary by the person creating the trust, moreover, dividends actually paid out of capital belong to the remainderman, and should be held for him, not paid out to the life tenant.42 liability by paying a particular creditor, or less than all the creditors).

§ 155. Rights of Majority. A corporation is pri marily, and of necessity, a matter of majority control.25 

The majority of the stockholders are entitled, in the absence of fraud or bad faith, to adopt such policies as they see fit, though they may not be the best or the wisest, and the courts will not interfere.26 They will not, however, be allowed to exercise their power to use the funds of the corporation for their own individual interests,27 or

This is the unavoidable result of the fundamental principle that the majority of the stockholders can regulate and control the lawful exercise of the powers conferred on a corporation by its charter."

§ 156. Minority Rights. The rule was formerly well nigh universal that equity had no jurisdiction to appoint a receiver to wind up the affairs of a corporation at suit of a minority stockholder.30 While the more modern doctrine is that equity has broad powers to protect minority stockholders where they have no other remedy, this power is exercised with great caution.32

Majority policies and control will not be interfered with merely because they are not in harmony with the views of the minority, or the best or wisest business policies, or not for the best interests of the corporation.88 Courts cannot be called upon to balance probabilities of profitable results as between different plans of corporate action proposed by or on behalf of different shareholders. "This is no business for any court to follow." The 

Evangelical Creed Congregation, 146 Wis. 610, 131 N. W. 353, 39 

L. R. A. (N. S.) 138, Ann. Cas. 

1913 C 376, to the effect that the majority may use funds of the corporation to defend their chosen course of conduct against attack by minority stockholders.

§ 159. Meetings In General. Such powers as the stockholders of a corporation have are collective and can only be exercised in meetings.59 They have no power as individuals, and even though a majority concur and express their assent in writing, their assent is not that of the corporation or binding upon it.6⁰ 

Stockholders' meetings may be either regular or special. The regular meeting is usually held at least annually, the time and place being fixed by the articles of incorporation or by-laws, but if not so fixed, annual meetings are held on the anniversaries of the first corporate meeting.61 By-laws may be, and usually are, passed governing the calling and conducting of all meetcient against general demurrer a complaint alleging demand by agent, but failing to state affirmatively that the agent was authorized).

§ 162. Liabilities-In General. As a general proposi tion, stockholders in a corporation are not liable for the debts or obligations of the corporations.89 One of the very objects of incorporation is to avoid personal liability.90 They are liable to the extent of their subscriptions to stock,91 and up to the par value of stock purchased but not paid for in full,92 or for the difference between par value and what they paid for watered or bonus stock.93 But creditors have no greater rights against subscribers or shareholders than has the corporation itself, except where the creditors have been misled by a pretense of the corporation that it has more capital than has in fact been paid in or received.

Where stockholders are liable upon unpaid subscriptions or for unpaid stock, the liability can be enforced only for the benefit of all creditors entitled, and is usually enforced in an action to wind up the affairs of the corporation,95 in which action all equities and contribution rights as between the various stockholders are subject to adjustment.96 The action should at least be on behalf of all creditors having like claims and against all stockholders liable, and also against the corporation, unless it has been dissolved or its assets wholly exhausted.97 

Power of the legislature to impose additional liabilities on stockholders as to obligations incurred after enactment of the law is said to be undoubted.98 But statutes imposing additional liability on stockholders are in derogation of the common law and are to be strictly construed; 99 and it has been held that an ordinary business corporation cannot validly amend its articles so as to impose liability for a one hundred per cent assessment on its stockholders, in the absence of statutory authority.¹

The personal liability thus imposed is of the same character as the common law liability of incorporators or organizers acting for a corporation before it attains legal existence. It is a primary and absolute liability, not to the corporation but to its creditors, and not dependent upon the amount of stock or continued ownership thereof, or solvency or insolvency of the corporation." In determining whether the requisite percentages have been subscribed and paid, oral subscriptions partially performed are to be included in the amount subscribed,16 but not oral subscriptions which have not been performed even in part on either side, as such subscriptions are within the provision of the statute of frauds as to sales of goods.17 The percentage required to be paid in, however, need not be paid in cash, but may be paid wholly or in part in labor or property.18 

Subscribers do not become "stockholders," so as to be personally liable as such, until their subscriptions have been accepted by the corporation.19

The statute is to be liberally construed in favor of laborers and employees.26 It extends further than to menial servants or manual laborers, and covers as well a factory superintendent and foreman paid on a daily wage basis,27 and services rendered without as well as within the state.28 The statute does not limit liability to wages for the last six months of service of the employee, though, even if it were so construed, there would be a presumption that payments by the corporation were applied to wages first earned, in the absence of any indication to the contrary.29 But the Wisconsin statute does not apply to foreign corporations, and courts of this state will not enforce the statute of another state imposing such liability.30
