§ 165. Actions Between Stockholders. Actions be tween stockholders do not ordinarily in any way affect the corporation and are governed by the usual rules as to actions and proceedings generally. Where the corporation is not a party to such an action, the defendant cannot counterclaim for services rendered to it, but one or both of the parties may, nevertheless, by virtue of the fact that both are stockholders, be estopped to set up irregularities in organization of the corporation after they have treated it as lawfully organized.36 

§ 166. Actions by Stockholders Against Corporation. 

One who deals with a corporation is not precluded, by reason of the fact that he owns stock therein, from proceeding against the corporation as a creditor or as an individual in respect of any liability to him personally.87 

But where a stockholder sues the corporation as such, he cannot deny its valid existence as a corporation.38

§ 168. -Necessity of Prior Demand on Corporation to Bring Suit. As a general proposition, a stockholder has no right to sue on behalf of the corporation until after he has first demanded that the corporation itself sue and his demand has been refused.54 It is immaterial that the corporation is a foreign corporation and has been dissolved, unless a showing is made that suit can no longer be brought in the corporate name.55 There is an exception to the general rule, however, and no preliminary demand on the corporation is necessary where it is obvious from circumstances that such a demand, if made, would be unavailing.56 Thus no demand is necessary where those against whom the action is to be brought control the board of directors so that an action, if brought and controlled by the board, would not be in good faith.57 But there is no absolute test as to when demand on the corporation is excused, and each case must rest on its own circumstances.58 It cannot be presumed that the president controls the directors or trustees, so

§ 169. -Parties. In an action brought by stock holders on behalf of the corporation, the corporation is at least a proper party defendant, and is sometimes referred to as a necessary defendant.62 The theory of joining the corporation is the old equitable doctrine that one who should be a coplaintiff, but refuses to join in bringing the action, may be made a defendant; or the corporation may be regarded as a trustee for its members, to be joined as a party to receive the benefit of the judgment on their behalf. Any stockholders other than the plaintiff and desiring to become parties to the action, may do so on application, though there is no formal statement in the complaint that the action is brought for for the benefit of all.64

§ 172. Ouster or Suspension of Members or Stock holders. It has been stated that, at common law, every corporation had the power of "amotion," or of expelling members.72 A business corporation, however, cannot expel its stockholders," and a statute or charter provision authorizing a nonbusiness corporation to expel or oust members is to be strictly construed. Although power to suspend or expel members exists, in the absence of statute or a valid charter provision, it can be exercised only for cause and after notice and hearing.75 The procedure may be governed to some extent by by-laws, although the charter is silent on the subject.76 The power to suspend or expel is not part of the general management of the corporation, however, but is confided in the body

(a) Officers Generally 

§ 173. In General. A corporation is merely an artificial creature of the law, or legal concept, having only a paper existence.¹ For this reason it must have officers or agents, or both; for it can act only through human agencies. Stockholders have but little to do with the actual management of the corporation, except to elect directors to act as a managing body, the directors, in turn, electing the president, secretary, treasurer and other officers. But whatever a corporation can do at all, whether rightfully or wrongfully, it can authorize an

§ 175. 

-To Stockholders. 

The officers of a corporation, as to its to its stockholders, are agents 23 and trustees 24 occupying a fiduciary relationship demanding the exercise of great good faith.25 In dealing with stockholders, an officer can take no advantage of his superior knowledge of affairs of the corporation and must fully and fairly disclose any information obtained by virtue of his position,26 particularly if the corporation is insolvent,27 or direct inquiry is made of the officer as to a matter within his knowledge. But if the required good faith is exercised and full disclosure made, so that the parties deal on an equal basis, there is no prohibition against transactions between an officer and a stockholder, and they are valid and binding.2

The officers of a corporation are not primarily liable to stockholders for misconduct or negligence in performance of their duties, liability in this connection being to the corporation. But if the corporation refuses or fails, on demand of a stockholder, to take steps to enforce the liability, the stockholders may maintain an action to that end on behalf of the corporation.³¹ 

§ 176. 

To Creditors. The officers of a corporation are often referred to as trustees for its creditors.32 The theory, however, that the assets of a corporation are a trust fund for its creditors has never gained a secure foothold in Wisconsin," and the officers of a corporation are not to be regarded as strict trustees for its creditors, but at most as "quasi" trustees, charged with the exercise of good faith in managing its affairs.4 The fiduciary relationship of the officers is primarily to the corporation, and only indirectly to the creditors.35

As in respect of stockholders,36 there is no primary liability to creditors for neglect of duties or mismanagealthough one purpose of the trust is sale of the entire stock of the corporation.

In one respect, the officers of a corporation are particularly bound to respect the rights of creditors. When a corporation is insolvent and has ceased to be a going concern, and its officers know, or should know, that suspension is pending, any transfer of property of the corporation to themselves in payment of debts due them as individuals from the corporation is a fraud in law and will not be permitted to stand as against the other creditors.42

The or by expressly undertaking individual liability. manager of a corporation may, moreover, be held liable for torts.45 Thus a managing officer having full charge and control and owning practically all of the stock, may be held liable for negligence in the management of a mill resulting in injury to an employee.46

An officer who signs a note is not liable thereon to the original payee where there was no intention either on his part or the payee's that he should be bound personally.47 The fact that a note reads "we promise to pay," and is signed with the corporate name and the name of an officer designated by his official title, does not make the officer personally liable. As a general proposition, addition of a title such as cashier, secretary, president, or agent, to the name of one signing a corporate name, sufficiently shows that he signs in his official capacity and only for the corporation, not as an individual.49 But where a note is signed by the officers of a corporation without designating their official capacities, and contains the promise of the corporation and "we, the undersigned" to pay, it must be construed as imposing liability on the individual signers as well as the corporation.50

[$ the corporation.66 There is no liability as matter of law, however, for misplaced confidence in employees and subordinates. While it is part of the duties of the officers to see that fairly accurate accounts are kept,68 they are not ordinarily bound to do this personally, and are chargeable with misconduct and misuse of funds by a subordinate only to the extent that a reasonably prudent man acting in the course of his duties might be expected to discover such things.69 A corporate officer is responsible only for failure to bring to the discharge of his duties the degree of attention, care, skill, and judgment ordinarily used and practiced in the discharge of duties such as he had, the degree of care, skill and judgment depending upon the subject to which it is to be applied, the particular circumstances of the case, and the usages of the business.70

§ 181. Control of Courts Over Duties and Manage ment. As a general proposition, the policy of courts toward the management of corporations is one of noninterference, or "hands off." This is due, not to want of power,81 but to sound discretion and the belief that it is not the function of the courts to take control away from those in whom it has been vested.82 The courts will interfere where those in control are plundering the corporation and mismanaging it to the verge of bankruptcy,88 but not merely because there is a disagreement as to business policy or in the absence of clear abuse of power, bad faith, or wilful abuse of discretion or positive fraud.84

§ 182. Authority-In General. to the same civil responsibility for their acts as individuals would be held for similar ones. If, through negligence, fraud, or mistake, a corporation causes injury to another, it must respond as must an individual. Since it can be negligent, fraudulent, or mistaken only through some agent, and since intentional authorization to an agent to make a mistake or state falsehood is hardly conceivable, the safety of business intercourse can only be protected by holding that, when a certain business or transaction is delegated to an agent, he becomes the corporation in conducting that business, and if he makes mistakes, is negligent, or commits fraud in so conducting it, the mistake, negligence, or fraud is committed by the corporation." 20

A corporation is accordingly liable for misrepresentations or fraud of its servants or agents, within the range of their duties, though there is no definite authority to defraud or make misstatements.21 It may even be held liable for malice,22 and is liable for negligence of servants and agents where an individual would be so liable by reason of relationship to a third person injured, there being a duty to exercise due care.28 Tort liability of a corporation is, however, more particularly discussed in a preceding chapter.24

§ 186. Knowledge Imputed to Corporation. The gen eral rule is thoroughly established that knowledge of an officer or agent is imputed to the corporation.27 This is, of course, but an application of a settled principle of the law of agency.28 But the general rule is subject to exception where knowledge is gained by an officer or agent when acting in furtherance of his own individual interests, for in such case he is not acting for the corporation.29 

The doctrine, moreover, does not go so far as to charge one agent of a corporation with all knowledge of another agent of the same corporation located at a distance,30 or to charge one corporation with facts known to an agent of another corporation because some of the officers or directors of the two corporations are the same.³¹

WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS § 187. Eligibility and Qualifications for Office. The existence of a provision requiring that officers or directors of a corporation be stockholders, does not disqualify those who hold stock merely in trust, or to whom stock is transferred for the sole purpose of qualifying them to act.32

By statute, the officers of a corporation holding stock in another corporation are made eligible for election as directors and officers of the latter.33 One may, moreover, become an officer de facto although not eligible to office, in the absence of objection to his functioning as an officer of the corporation or the taking of legal proceedings to test his right to office.34 But where an ineligible person is elected, and the by-laws or charter provide that an officer shall continue in office until his successor is regularly elected and qualified, the old officer may bring direct proceedings to oust his ineligible successor. 85 While there is a general requirement, save as to railroads, that the principal managing officer or superintendent reside within the state, nonresidence of officers concerns only the state and the right of a nonresident to hold office can be tested only in an appropriate proceeding.37

[§ These provisions are construed as vesting power to elect all officers in the directors. The articles of incorporation can accordingly merely designate the officers which the corporation shall have; they cannot empower the stockholders to elect them, or any of them.40 It has also been said that no officer can be legally elected until one-half the stock has been subscribed and one-fifth paid in.¹¹ But one who is acting as an officer of the corporation, recognized as such by the corporation, and in possession of the incidents of office, must be recognized as an officer by outsiders in the absence of a direct attack by proceedings proper to question his title to office, regardless of defects in his election.42

It appears that a contract between organizers of a corporation and the corporation that each organizer is to hold an office for five years at a fixed salary, is void if in contravention of a by-law calling for annual election of officers. Our supreme court has said that if the right to hold office as president of a corporation can be acquired and held by contract with the corporation under any circumstances, the contract must at least be clear and express.44

§ 190. Compensation for Services. As a general prop osition, an officer of a corporation, who is a stockholder, is not entitled to compensation for services as officer in the absence of an express contract or provision to that effect.55 But compensation may be allowed by by-law 56 or by agreement. An officer and director of a corporation cannot legally, as director, fix his own salary as officer,5 though the stockholders may ratify such fixation so that neither they nor the corporation can question it.58 Where there is a right to compensation, moreover, it may be forfeited by misappropriation of funds or other misconduct so gross as to warrant removal from office,59 and no extra compensation can be charged for services within the line of duty for which a salary is paid.⁰

§ 194. Vice President. The vice president of a cor poration is usually not endowed with large powers, either actually or ostensibly, and is often practically a nonentity so far as conduct of the business of the corporation is concerned.92 But when the president is away or unable to act, the vice president has his powers, 98 and if the vice president is the only officer of the corporation in the state and manages the affairs of the corporation in Wisconsin, third persons are justified in assuming that he has a considerable range of authority.94 No proof is necessary that the vice president of a corporation, indorsing a note for the corporation, had authority to do so; 95 but there is no presumption that such an officer has authority to sell its real estate.96

§ 195. Secretary and Treasurer. The authority and powers of the secretary of a corporation, like those of the president, are such as are given to him by the articles of organization, by-laws, and acts of the board of directors. In addition, the corporation is estopped to deny, as to third persons, such apparent authority as it allows him to assume and exercise.97 He may thus have, or be clothed with, much the same powers and authority as the president, with interchangeable duties in many respects and powers including general management,98 and may be the financial manager of the business.99 His indorsement for the corporation of a note made to it is presumptively valid and authorized.¹ But the secretary has no authority, merely by virtue of his office, to execute a judgment note on behalf of the corporation."

The secretary of a corporation, like its other officers,³ owes it the utmost fidelity and, in dealing with the corporation, must exercise the highest good faith.

§ 198. Dealing with Corporation or Stockholders. In dealing with the corporation or with a stockholder thereof, a director, like officers of the corporation generally,25 will not be permitted to make and retain secret profits,26 and must fully and fairly disclose all information within his knowledge and take no advantage of his position.27

§ 199. Furthering Individual or Conflicting Interests. 

Directors are not permitted to use their position to further their own private or individual interests, or the interests of third persons,30 or to obtain any advantage over the corporation,31 being bound to manage the affairs of the corporation so as to promote the common interests of those concerned therein.82 They accordingly have no right to squander or give away assets. In so far as they attempt to act for their own individual benefit or interest, and against that of the corporation, their acts are not binding upon the corporation.84 There is no rule, however, preventing a director from purchasing obligations of the corporation at a discount and enforcing them for the full amount against the corporation, if at the time of the purchase the corporation was not in a position to buy or settle the debt.85

§ 204. Resignation or Removal. The filing of a writ ten resignation by a director immediately creates a vacancy on the board, notwithstanding the by-laws provide that directors shall hold office until their successors are duly elected.69 

Quo warranto proceedings, to remove or test the right to office of directors, cannot succeed if the ground for questioning their election is a challenge of the validity of stock voted for them. There must first be an equitable action to test the validity of the stock. But the procedure may be reversed, and an equitable proceeding brought to test the stock, and equity having obtained jurisdiction for one purpose, will then proceed, in the same suit and as incidental relief, to remove or enjoin the directors from acting.70

Where removal of directors is sought on grounds of incompetency, it is a strong circumstance against the petitioner that under their management the concern has steadily grown and prospered."¹

Voting and Resolutions. § 207. In General. There is no substantial distinction between rights and remedies of corporations and those of individuals,' except as restrictions are placed upon recourse to the courts by foreign corporations in respect of business transacted in the state without a license, and as rights of action are denied upon obligations contracted with others than members before fifty per cent of the stock has been subscribed and twenty per cent paid. By statute, domestic corporations are expressly empowered to sue and be sued, and to appear and defend in all actions and proceedings, in the corporate name, to the same extent as a natural person. § 209. Venue. The venue or proper place of trial of actions against corporations generally is the county in which the corporation is situated or has its principal office or place of business, "or in which the cause of action or some part thereof arose." 18 One suing a corporation accordingly has an absolute choice to sue it either in the county where it has its principal office or where the cause arose.14 If neither such county is chosen, however, the corporation has a right to demand a change of venue to a proper county.15 While prejudice or interest of the judge may be ground for change of venue, the fact that the judge was one of the original incorporators and directors is not ground unless it is further shown that he is still interested in the corporation,16 and our supreme court has said that it is difficult to perceive how a judge could be prejudiced against a corporation personally."7

Determination of where the "cause of action, or some part thereof, arose," is not always a simple matter.18 

It may be assumed, in the absence of contrary allegations, that a cause of action, the primary purpose of which is to enforce liability of officers of the corporation but in respect of which the corporation is made a defendant because of failure or refusal to sue, arose at the principal office of the corporation, where the basis of the action is a long series of fraudulent acts on the part of the officers. 19 § 210. Summons. A corporation is beyond question a "person" within constitutional prohibitions against deprivation of property without due process of law.20 Statutory provisions for service on corporations must, therefore, accord "due process," or they are unconstitutional and void.21 But a corporation, not being a flesh and blood person but only a creature of the law, can only be reached by process through the medium of some human agency. 

For this reason, this must of necessity be served through its officers, agents or servants, or someone appointed to receive service for it, and statutes making reasonable provisions of this nature accord due process and are not unconstitutional.22 The rule is particularly exacting with reference to corporations that when a particular method

§ 211. Parties. The rules as to parties in actions by and against corporations are the same as in other cases.36 

The corporation may be joined as a defendant in an action for fraud by its officers and agents in the sale of stock,87 or where the officers have mingled their own property with that of the corporation,38 or where an action is brought on behalf of the corporation by a stockholder or creditor after the management has refused to enforce its rights.39 It should be made a party whenever the corporate interests will be affected by the action.40 

If the corporation is a necessary or proper party defendant, failure to join it as such cannot be excused on the ground that its officers are already parties.$1

§ 213. Discovery and Depositions. Corporations are subject to substantially the same rules in respect of adverse examination or discovery proceedings and depositions, as are private individuals.56 To place them on the same basis as individuals in these respects, the statutes provide for adverse examination of the existing and also former officers, agents or employees of corporate parties, and the examination of such representatives or employees is conducted under the same rules which govern examination of an individual party,58 its scope being largely within the discretion of the trial court.59 57

§ 214. Evidence and Witnesses. The general rules as to presumptions, and burden of proof, and governing the admissibility of evidence are applicable in actions by and against corporations. Thus, in an action by an officer of a corporation suing as an individual, a general denial by the defendant puts plaintiff upon proof that the contract sued on was with him and not with the corporation of which he is an officer.61 But admissions of officers and members of a corporation, or of its agents, do not bind the corporation and are not admissible against it, unless they were authorized to speak on its behalf.82 

As to testimony to transactions had with a person since deceased, officers and stockholders of a corporation are now incompetent to testify on behalf of the corporation the same as natural persons are incompetent to testify on their own behalf to such transactions, though the rule was otherwise prior to a 1907 amendment of the governing statute. § 216. Appeal and Review. Statutes authorizing ap peals obviously apply to corporations as well as to natural persons, in the absence of language showing a contrary intention. The right to appeal is not lost because of insolvency or because the corporation has suspended business for so long a time that it might be adjudged dissolved.75 In view of the circumstance, moreover, that a corporation can only appeal through the act of some human agency, authority of one who appeals for it is presumed.78

Failure of a corporation to prove its due incorporation is no ground for reversal where the failure to make such proof was not raised in the lower court.”

§ 220. Assignments for Benefit of Creditors. The right to make a voluntary assignment for the benefit of creditors, when not forbidden by statute, is inherent in a corporation as well as in an individual,20 and is not affected by the existence of statutory authority for general winding up or liquidation proceedings.1 In fact, after a corporation has made a voluntary assignment it is too late to start proceedings against it under the sequestration and winding-up statute, as its property and assets are already in the hands of the assignee and beyond reach.22 The board of directors may make such an assignment without special authority from or consent of the stockholders, in the absence of a charter provision or statutory requirement to the contrary. The assignee of an insolvent corporation represents the creditors, not the stockholders.25 He is entitled to all the assets,26 including sums recovered in an action brought by a creditor against officers of the corporation to compel them to make good moneys dissipated by negligent management,27 and should therefore be made a party in his official capacity to any such action.28 The assignee may himself maintain suit to enforce liability of officers for mismanagement or neglect of duty, and is charged with the duty of collecting in the assets, including balances due on unpaid stock subscriptions.29 After an assignment for the benefit of creditors has been made, creditors can accordingly obtain the benefit of subscription liabilities only by assenting to or becoming parties to the assignment. 80 The fact that the person to whom the assignment is made was formerly a stockholder and officer of the corporation does not affect his competency to act, where he asserts no claims against the corporation and has sold out his stock and resigned his office.³¹ § 221. will be appointed only when the corporation is insolvent and at the instance of creditors; 80 never will a receivership be imposed lightly.81 As hereinbefore shown, the courts are very reluctant to interfere with the management of a corporation, realizing that by reason of the cumbersomeness of judicial machinery they are not equipped for the task, and further quite properly recognizing that the theory of corporate management is control of the majority, and that those having the greatest financial interest at stake have the right to manage their own affairs and to make experiments and even mistakes.82

A receiver accordingly will not be appointed at the instance of minority stockholders merely because of a disagreement as to business policies.88 Whether such a step is proper because of a deadlock in management or between evenly divided groups of stockholders has not been directly decided.84 No appointment will be made on that ground where plaintiff is chargeable with unreasonableness responsible for the deadlock, or there is no danger of irreparable loss from the existing situation.85 But a receivership is proper if the assets of the corporation, through mismanagement, collusion and fraud, are in danger of loss,86 or the officers are mismanaging the corporation to the verge of bankruptcy and so that the purposes for which it was organized are no longer obtainable.87

§ 228. -Appointment, Rights and Duties. A re ceiver should not be appointed for a corporation without notice to it, unless the emergency is great and loss so imminent as to brook no delay. Save in such circumstances, an ex parte appointment is improvident and the court has no discretion but to vacate it on application.89 

But the regularity and propriety of appointment of a receiver is not open to collateral attack in an action brought by him,90

Even though a second sequestration proceeding is instituted in another court after one such proceeding has already been begun, the receiver appointed in the subsequent suit is at least a receiver de facto whose lawful acts and contracts are to be recognized as binding and who is entitled to just compensation for his services up to the time his authority is regularly ended.91 

A receiver in sequestration proceedings is a trustee of the assets in the right of the corporation for the benefit of its creditors. His duty is to them and he should act accordingly.92

§ 230. Dissolution-In General. Dissolution of a cor poration may occur either voluntarily, by surrender of its charter and acceptance thereof by the state, or involuntarily, by forfeiture of its rights and franchises¹ or against the will of its members. It may also occur by termination of the period for which its charter was granted without renewal of the same.

§ 232. -Effect Generally. The effect of taking the steps required for dissolution is not immediately to terminate the existence of the corporation for all purposes.

Eminent authorities on the common law, such as Bacon, Kyd and Kent, have declared that debts of a corporation were extinguished upon termination of its lawful existence, and its real estate reverted to the grantor and its personalty to the sovereign. It has been held that the fact that a corporate grantor has been dissolved does not affect the right of persons entitled to the benefit of a restrictive covenant, in respect of real estate, to enforce the covenant, though it provides for reversion of the property to the grantor in case of breach.24

§ 236. Forfeiture of Franchise-In General. For feiture of a corporate charter, like other forfeitures, is not favored in the law. The statutes provide: “Whenever any corporation shall have remained insolvent, or shall have neglected or refused to pay and discharge its notes or other evidences of debt, or shall have suspended its ordinary business for one year, it shall be deemed to have surrendered the rights, privileges and franchises granted or acquired under any law, and shall, in a proper action, be adjudged to be dissolved." This provision, however, in view of the reluctance of courts in respect of forfeitures, is not construed as ipso facto dissolving the corporation in cases within its terms, but as merely authorizing its dissolution in a proper action. CHAPTER 14 MERGER, CONSOLIDATION AND REORGANIZATION § 239. Merger and Consolidation Generally. 

§ 240. Effect of Merger or Consolidation. 

§ 241. Reorganizations. 

The § 239. Merger and Consolidation Generally. 

terms "consolidation" and "merger" are often used somewhat loosely, and sometimes as synonymous. It is well settled, however, that merger is not the same thing as consolidation. A "merger" takes place where a corporation, remaining in being, merges in itself one or more other corporations. In a consolidation, on the other hand, corporations entering into the arrangement are dissolved and a new corporation formed out of the elements of the old ones.¹

Not every arrangement between corporations, furthermore, constitutes a consolidation or merger. Thus it is neither a consolidation nor a merger where stockholders in different corporations merely agree to exchange stock, though the design is to unify management, if continued independent existence of each of the corporations is contemplated. The same is true of a transfer of property from an existing corporation to a new corporation largely composed of members of the old, independent corporate existences being thereafter maintained. When one corporation purchases all the property and salable franchises of another, the arrangement may properly be 

1 Union Indemnity Co. v. Rail road Commission, 187 Wis. 528, 205 N. W. 492. 

2 Union Indemnity Co. v. Rail road Commission, 187 Wis. 528, 205 N. W. 492. 

8 Wegner 

V. Sheboygan-Elkhart Lake Ry. & Elec. Co., 171 

Wis. 325, 176 N. W. 865. 275

§ 240] 

WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS 

termed a "succession," and is not a consolidation or merger unless there is something further than the mere purchase and sale to give it such character.ª 

There can be neither a consolidation nor a merger in the absence of legislative authority, nor where, though such authority exists, there is not even a colorable compliance with the statutes. It is immaterial in such instances that there has been an attempt to consolidate and some steps have been taken to that end.5 

§ 240. Effect of Merger or Consolidation. Where a corporation goes out of existence by being annexed to or merged in another, no arrangements being made for payment of liabilities of the former, the latter is responsible upon all its obligations upon the equitable ground that otherwise the transfer would be in fraud of creditors."

As shown in the preceding section, however, there is no merger by mere purchase of the assets of another corporation, and accordingly there is no implied assumption of liabilities. Where the purchase is at a foreclosure or judicial sale, it is particularly clear that there is no implied assumption of obligations, notwithstanding statutory provisions authorizing the purchasers of corporate property and rights at such a sale to carry on the business or to incorporate for that purpose, as otherwise there would be a deprivation of the legitimate rights of a purchaser at foreclosure or judicial sale to take the property free and clear.8

While there is no doubt that a corporation has the right, in so far as the state of its creation is concerned, to transact business in other states or countries,¹ and may do business without restriction from other states as long as it stays within the protection of the interstate commerce clause of the Federal Constitution and does only inter-

The question usually involved is: What constitutes interstate business?-for in respect of such business a state has no control, the regulation of interstate commerce, under the Constitution of the United States, being solely the function of the federal government and the states having no power to interfere therewith. Probably no all-embracing rule can be laid down.17 Each instance depends upon the particular facts involved.18 A corporation may be doing intrastate business though it has no resident agent in the state. 19 It has been held to constitute doing business within the state to place advertising for a Wisconsin company in Wisconsin,20 or to issue in Wisconsin a policy of insurance written outside the state.21 But it is not transacting business within the state merely to send a note into the state for collection by a local bank,22 or to send into the state a muniment of title to be held until paid for pursuant to a contract executed in another state, or give a course of instruction by correspondence. 28 24 Usually, where a contract is entered into and is to be performed wholly outside the state it does not constitute doing business within the state.25 While single or oc-

§ 246. -Sales. Ordinarily, selling goods from a stock maintained in Wisconsin is doing business in the state and not within the protection of interstate commerce. § 249. Validity of Contracts and Transactions of Unlicensed Corporation-In General. The statutes provide that every contract made by or on behalf of any foreign corporation doing business in this state, "affecting the personal liability thereof or relating to property within this state," before it has taken out a license to do business "shall be wholly void on its behalf and on behalf of its assigns, but shall be enforceable against it or them." This provision, obviously, has no application to interstate transactions and must be construed as though it expressly excluded such transactions, first, because the states have no control over interstate commerce, and second, because interstate transactions are not "doing business in the state." 65 Subject to this im-

In addition to what may be referred to for purposes of convenience as the "void-contract" statute, the statutes provide generally that no unlicensed foreign corporation shall "transact business or acquire, hold, or dispose of property in this state," 78 thus making any dealing within the language quoted, though not within the void-contract statute, illegal and against public policy, unless protected as interstate commerce."

The void-contract provision, it will be noted, does not cover all contracts, but only those made by a corporation transacting business within the state and which either "affect its liability" or relate to "property within this state." 75 It does not apply to a contract made or a lien acquired upon property outside the state by a corporation not “transacting business within the state” at the time of the particular deal.76 Contracts affecting the liability of the corporation do not include all contracts for the breach of which the corporation may be liable in damages or otherwise," and the provision does not affect collection by a foreign corporation of bills and notes, or in respect of contracts fully executed outside the state, or enforcement of any contract not by its stipulations imposing duties or liabilities upon the corporation and not merely incidental to a transaction imposing duties or liabilities; 78 although if any such contract "relates to

-Transfers of Property. § 252. Reports and Annual Fees. Not only must a foreign corporation take out a license and pay a fee in order to do noninterstate business within the state, but it must further make annual reports and pay an annual fee within the time allowed by law or its existing license becomes void. For purposes of determining the license fee, the words "capital stock" as used in the statute refer to actual, or issued and paid for stock, not authorized capital. Failure to pay the license fee for one year does not affect the validity of a license actually issued for a subsequent year. Payment of fees evaded in years past, may, however, be made a condition to granting a license for a particular year, and mandamus will not issue to compel granting of a license even where it is held up to compel payment of arrearages beyond the statute of limitations. 5

[§ 254 "liabilities and restrictions" imposed upon domestic corporations of like character, and has no other or greater powers.16 The purpose of the statute so providing, which was adopted from a similar provision in Illinois,17 was "to produce uniformity in the powers, liabilities, duties and restrictions of foreign and domestic corporations of like character and bring them all under the influence of the same law." 18 Provisions of law referring only to "corporations," and not by their nature inapplicable to foreign corporations, are accordingly construed as applicable to the latter as well as to domestic corporations.19 Thus foreign corporations cannot validly sell stock having par value for less than par.20 In addition to restriction to powers of like domestic corporations a foreign corporation is, of course, likewise restricted by its charter and any limitations placed upon its power in the state of its organization.21 That such a corporation has acted beyond powers conferred by the state of its creation, however, is, as a general rule, open to question only by persons directly interested in the corporation or by the state whose charter and franchises are being exceeded and abused.22

§ 255] WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS § 255. Actions-In General. As a general proposi tion, a foreign corporation licensed to do business in the state may sue or be sued,28 the same as a domestic corporation. Even though the corporation is unlicensed, there is nothing to prohibit it from maintaining a tort action,25 and it may use the Wisconsin courts to enforce rights against a local debtor,26 or to recover personal property,27 unless the effect would be to give force to a contract affecting its personal liability or relating to property within the state.28 The statutes provide generally that "a corporation created by or under the laws of any other state or county or of the United States may prosecute or defend an action or proceeding in the courts of this state in the same manner as corporations created under the laws of this state, except as otherwise specially prescribed by law." 29 This provision is merely a codification of a rule which would obtain in any event,30 on principles of interstate comity; 31 but the right

§ 256. -Against the Corporation. It is not burden ing interstate commerce to subject corporations doing a purely interstate business to process of a state wherein part of the business is transacted. Particularly where litigation is in respect of property within the state, a foreign corporation, though not licensed, must recognize the jurisdiction of Wisconsin courts, if accorded due process of law.38 Attachment of its property is available against a foreign corporation, though it has no office in the state,89 and such a corporation is subject to garnishment process if it has property within the state or the cause of action arose here.40 It has been declared no abuse of judicial discretion to entertain an action against a foreign corporation by a nonresident even in respect of a cause of action arising elsewhere, though there is perhaps no absolute right to use the Wisconsin courts in such case. Interesting questions sometimes arise as to whether one is an "agent" acting or selling for the corporation or an independent dealer merely purchasing goods from it for resale. There is no right to serve a foreign corporation by publication where it has taken out a license to do business and no reason is shown why service cannot be made on the secretary of state."1

A general appearance by a foreign corporation, of course, waives defective service of process upon it in like manner as such an appearance by an individual.72 

The venue or place of trial of actions against foreign corporations is governed by the general provision fixing the place for trial of actions against corporations "existing under the law of this state." 78 

§ 260. -Discovery or Adverse Examination. § 261. 

-Pleading, Defenses and Evidence. As a general proposition, pleading in actions by and against foreign corporations is the same as in other cases. 77 

While the fact of incorporation must be averred, it is sufficient merely to state that the plaintiff or defendant is a foreign corporation.78 Incorporation need not be proved unless denied as required in the case of a domestic corporation to put the opposite party on proof thereof.79 If advantage is sought to be taken of the fact that the corporation has not taken out a license to do business in the state, and that therefore it cannot enforce a contract upon. which it sues, the requisite facts to make out such a defense must be alleged,80 and the burden of proof is on the party alleging them.81 In an action to recover a penalty for failure to file statements and reports, the complaint must show all facts necessary to make the duty to file a statement appear.82

1 Furnished by the secretary of state on application. The articles must be in duplicate, an original and a duly verified copy, and the secretary of state appropriately supplies them in duplicate, one set containing an appropriate verification. 

2 Great care should be taken in the statement of purposes and objects, following suggestions set forth in the text, § 34, supra. In incorporating under chapter 180, Statutes, the purposes must of course be limited to those permitted by that chapter, and if the object is an insurance agency, for example, powers cannot be made so broad as to include the carrying on of a general insurance business. (See comments of Joseph R. Edwards, 19 Wisconsin Bar Ass'n Reports 170.) Many purpose provisions which will serve as general guides are set forth in subsequent forms.

The principal duties of the Secretary shall be to countersign all deeds, leases and conveyances executed by the corporation, affix the seal of the corporation thereto, and to such other papers as shall be required or directed to be sealed, and to keep a record of the proceedings of the Board of Directors, and to safely and systematically keep all books, papers, records and documents belonging to the corporation, or in any wise pertaining to the business thereof. 

The principal duties of the Treasurer shall be to keep and account for all moneys, credits and property, of any and every nature, of the corporation, which shall come into his hands, and keep an accurate account of all moneys received and disbursed, and proper vouchers for moneys disbursed, and to render such accounts, statements and inventories of moneys received and disbursed, and of money and property on hand, and generally of all matters pertaining to this office, as shall be required by the Board of Directors.

If nonpar stock is provided for, it will be issued for the consideration fixed by the stockholders, unless the articles authorize the directors to fix the consideration. A provision now recommended by the office of the secretary of state where there is to be nonpar stock is as follows: "Such no par value stock may be issued by the corporation from time to time for such consideration as may be fixed from time to time by the Board of Directors thereof, and any and all shares so issued, the fixed consideration for which has been paid or delivered, shall be deemed fully paid stock and not liable for any further call or assessment thereon, and the holder of such stock shall not be liable for any further payment.' 

Where all the capital stock is nonpar, or to the extent that it is composed of such stock, capital should not be stated in dollars, but in number of shares. 322

No. 22. Articles of Organization—Massachusetts Trust or Joint Stock Company. 

(See the form set forth in the reported decision in Baker v. Stern, 194 Wis. 233, 216 N. W. 147, 58 A. L. R. 462, beginning at p. 236.)

No. 23. Articles of Organization-Provision That Specific Powers Shall Not Limit General Powers. 

In furtherance, and not in limitation of the general powers conferred by the laws of the state of Wisconsin, and by the principles of the common law, upon corporations organized under the provisions of law authorizing the formation of this corporation, and of the purposes and powers herein before stated, the corporation shall also have the following purposes and powers, it being expressly provided that the enumeration of specific powers shall not be construed to limit or restrict in any manner the aforesaid general powers of the corporation.

No. 24. Articles of Organization-General Provision for Ownership of Property. 

To purchase or otherwise acquire, own and hold unlimitedly such real and personal property of every kind and description within and without the state of Wisconsin, and in any part of the world, suitable, necessary, useful or advisable in connection with any or all of the objects hereinbefore or hereinafter set forth, and to convey, sell, assign, transfer, lease, mortgage, pledge, exchange or otherwise dispose of any of such property. 

No. 25. Articles of Organization—Provision for Acquiring Patents. 

To purchase or otherwise acquire any and all letters patent and similar rights granted by the United States or any other country or government, licenses and the like, or any other interests therein, or any inventions which may seem capable of being used for or in connection with any of the objects or purposes of said corporation, and 331

No. 26] 

WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS 

to use, develop, sell and grant licenses in respect to or other interests in the same, and otherwise turn the same to account. 

No. 26. Articles of Organization-Provision for Acquiring Copy rights, Trade-Marks, etc.

To purchase, acquire, apply for, register, secure, hold, own, or sell, or otherwise dispose of, any and all copyrights, trade-marks, trade names and distinctive marks.

No. 27. Articles of Organization-Provision for Power to Act as 

Agents, Trustees, etc.

To act as agents, contractors, trustees, or otherwise, and either alone or in company with others, as fully and to the same extent as natural persons might or could do and in any part of the world. 

No. 28. Articles of Organization-Provision for Aiding and Financing Others. 

To raise and assist in raising money for, and to aid, by way of bonus, loan, promise, indorsement, guaranty of bonds, debentures or other securities or otherwise, any other company or corporation, and to guarantee the performance of contracts by any such company, corporation or by any other person or persons with whom the company may have business relations. 

No. 29. Articles of Organization-Provisions for Aid and Pensions to Employees.

To establish and support or aid in the establishment and support of associations, institutions, funds, trusts and conveniences calculated to benefit employees or ex-employees of the company (or its predecessors in the business) or the dependents or connections, of such persons, and to grant pensions and allowances, and to make payments towards insurance, and to subscribe or guarantee money for charitable or benevolent objects, or for any exhibition, or for any public, general or useful object.

No. 30. Articles of Organization-Provisions for Carrying on Other 

Business.

To carry on any other business, whether manufacturing or otherwise, which may seem to the company, capable of being conveniently carried on in connection with its business or calculated directly or 332

No. 31. Articles of Organization-Provision for Branching Into Allied Projects. 

To purchase, hire, make, construct or otherwise acquire, provide, maintain, equip, alter, erect, improve, repair, manage, work and operate any private roads, private telegraph and telephone lines, bridges, piers, wharves, wells, reservoirs, flumes, watercourses, waterworks, aqueducts, shafts, tunnels, furnaces, coke ovens, crushing works, gas works, electric light and power plants, compressed air plants, chemical works of all kinds, concentrators, smelters, smelting plants and refineries, matting plants, warehouses, workshops, factories, dwelling houses, stores, hotels or other buildings, engines, machinery, implements and other works, conveniences and properties of any description in connection with or which may seem directly or indirectly conducive to any of the objects of the company, and to contribute to, subsidize or otherwise aid or take part in any such operations. 

No. 32. Articles of Organization—Provision for Entering Partnership or Working Agreement. 

To enter into partnership or into any arrangement for sharing of profits, union of interests, co-operation, joint adventure, reciprocal concession or otherwise, with any persons or company carrying on or engaged in or about to carry on or engage in any business or transaction which the company is authorized to carry on or engage in, or any business or transaction capable of being conducted so as directly or indirectly to benefit the company; and to lend money to, guarantee the contracts of, or otherwise assist any such person or company, and to take or otherwise acquire shares and securities of any such company, and to sell, hold, reissue, with or without guaranty, or otherwise deal with the same.

No. 36. Articles of Organization-Restriction on Sale or Transfer of Stock. 

No shares of stock in this corporation shall be transferable by stockholders indebted to this corporation until such indebtedness is paid in full.

No. 37. Articles of Organization-Same-Another Form. 

The subscriptions for and the ownership of all shares of stock in this corporation are made and taken upon the condition that any holder of shares of stock desiring to sell the same shall first offer his stock to the corporation at his lowest price and the corporation shall have days in which to exercise its option to purchase the same. Said notice shall be given by a letter addressed to the home office of this corporation at No. Street, On its failure to exercise its option within said days, the stockholders of this corporation shall have days to exercise their option to purchase said stock at days, the stocksaid price. After the expiration of said holder shall be free to make any other sale of his stock. 

No. 38. Articles of Organization-Same-Another Form. 

Shares of stock in this corporation shall not be transferred or sold until said sale or transfer shall have been reported to the directors and approved by them.

No. 39. Articles of Organization-Same-Another Form. 

If at any time any of the original stockholders desire to sell and dispose of their stock, said stockholder or stockholders shall first offer it in writing to the board of directors, stating prices and terms, and give the board of directors ten days in which to place it with the stockholders. At the expiration of ten days if no stockholder has purchased and settled for same, said stockholder or stockholders shall have the right to sell to whoever will purchase for the same sums and prices for which it was offered to the board of directors. 

No. 40. Articles of Organization—Provisions as to Preferred Stock. 

The holders of the preferred stock shall be entitled to cumulative dividends thereon at the rate of six dollars ($6.00) per share or six per centum of the amount of par value for each and every fiscal year of the life of the corporation and no more, payable out of any 335

No. 41] WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS 

and all surplus or net profits, quarterly, half-yearly or yearly, as and when declared by the board of directors, before any dividends shall be declared, set apart for, or paid upon the common stock of the corporations. Said dividends on the preferred stock shall be cumulative, so that if the corporation shall fail in any fiscal year to pay such dividends on all of the issued and outstanding preferred stock, such deficiency in the dividends shall be fully paid, but without interest, before any dividends shall be paid or set apart on the common stock. Subject to the foregoing provisions said preferred stock shall not be entitled to participate in any other or additional earnings or profits of the corporation.

No. 41. Articles of Organization-Same-Redemption Provision. 

The whole of the preferred stock may be redeemed on any dividend day at the option of the board of directors, upon sixty (60) days' notice by mail to the holders of record of such stock as may be prescribed by the by-laws, or, in the absence of any by-laws upon the subject, by resolution of its board of directors, by paying for each share of the preferred stock one hundred and fifteen dollars ($115) in cash, and in addition thereto all unpaid dividends accrued thereon at the date fixed for such redemption. 

No. 42. Articles of Organization-Same-Option to Convert to Common Stock. 

Any registered holder of preferred stock of this company may, subject to the approval of the directors, elect to have such shares of preferred stock held by him and registered in his name, or any of them, converted into common stock aforesaid. Such election shall be declared by notice in writing to the company, signed by such holder and accompanied by the certificate or certificates of the preferred stock so as to be converted, and the board of directors shall thereupon adopt a resolution that such conversation be approved and have effect accordingly, and thereupon the certificate for said shares of preferred stock shall be canceled, and the requisite alterations shall be made in the transfer and stock books, and a certificate for the proper amount of a common stock shall thereupon be executed and delivered to such stockholder.

No. 43. Articles of Organization-Same-Rights on Dissolution. 

In the event of the dissolution or liquidation of the corporation, or a sale of all its assets (whether voluntary or involuntary) or in 336

FORMS 

[No. 47 event of its insolvency or upon any distribution of its capital, there shall be paid to the holders of the preferred stock the par value thereof, to wit, one hundred dollars ($100) per share and the amount of all unpaid accrued dividends thereon, before any sum shall be paid or any assets distributed among the holders of the common stock; and after the payment to the holders of the preferred stock of its par value and the unpaid accrued dividends thereon, the remaining assets and funds of the corporation shall be divided among and paid to the holders of the common stock according to their respective shares. 

No. 44. Articles of Organization—Provision as to Eligibility to Office. 

To be eligible to any of the above named offices of this corporation, a person must be the owner of at least shares of the capital stock of this corporation, as shown by the books of the corporation and any person duly qualified may hold one or more offices in the corporation. 

No. 45. Articles of Organization—Provision for Removal of Officers. 

Any officer or director of this corporation may be removed at any stockholders' meeting called for the purpose by a majority vote of the outstanding capital stock of the corporation. 

No. 46. Articles of Organization-Same-Another Form. 

Any officer elected or appointed by the board of directors may be removed at any time by the affirmative vote of a majority of the whole board of directors. Any other officer or employee of the company may be removed at any time by vote of the board of directors, or any committee or superior officer upon whom such power of removal may be conferred by the by-laws or by vote of the board of directors.

No. 47. Articles of Organization-Provision as to Resignation of 

Officers.

Any officer may resign by filing a written resignation with the secretary of the corporation, such resignation to take effect five days. after the receipt thereof by the secretary if it is not sooner accepted by regular action of the board of directors. 337

No. 49. Articles of Organization—Provision Empowering Directors to Appoint Committees and Agents. 

The board of directors of this corporation shall have power to appoint such committees and agents for the carrying out of the work of this corporation as they deem for the best interests of the corporation and may invest such committees and agents with such powers in the management of such corporation as the board may deem for the best interests of the corporation.

No. 50. Articles of Organization—Provision for Executive Committee. 

The board of directors shall have power by a resolution passed by a majority vote of the whole board, under suitable provision of the by-laws, to designate two or more of their number to constitute an executive committee, which committee shall for the time being, as 338

FORMS 

[No. 54 provided in said resolution, or in the by-laws, have and exercise all the powers of the board of directors which may be lawfully delegated in the management of the business and affairs of the company, and shall have power to authorize the seal of the company to be affixed to all papers which may require it. 

No. 51. Articles of Organization-Provision for Directors to Make or Alter By-Laws. 

Subject always to by-laws made by the stockholders, the board of directors may make by-laws, and, from time to time, may alter, amend or repeal any by-laws; but any by-laws made by the board of directors may be altered or repealed by the stockholders at any annual meeting, or at any special meeting, provided notice of each proposed alteration or repeal by the stockholders be included in the notice of the meeting of the stockholders.

No. 52. Articles of Organization-Provision Allowing Directors to Vote Though Interested. 

In the absence of actual fraud, no contract made or other action taken by the concurrent votes of a majority of the entire number of directors shall be invalid or voidable by reason of the fact that some or all of the directors are interested, nor shall any director be incapacitated from voting upon such contract or with respect to any such action by reason of such interest.

No. 53. Articles of Organization—Provision for Cumulative Voting on Directors.

At all elections of directors of this corporation each stockholder shall be entitled to as many votes as shall equal the number of his shares of stock, multiplied by the number of directors to be elected, and he may cast all of such votes for a single director or may distribute them among the number to be voted for, or any two or more of them, as he may see fit.

No. 54. Articles of Organization-Provision as to Eligibility of 

Directors.

No person shall be eligible to become or to remain a director of this corporation if he, or any member of his immediate family, shall be directly or indirectly interested either as owner, partner, stockholder, officer, director, agent, employee, attorney, lender of money, 339

No. 55] 

WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS 

beneficiary, trustee, or otherwise in any business which competes with or is antagonistic to the business of this corporation. No attorney, agent, employee, partner, trustee, or member of the immediate family of any person who is or becomes ineligible, under the above provisions, shall be eligible to become, or remain, a director of this corporation. 

No. 55. Articles of Organization-Provision for Calls and Assessments. 

The directors may from time to time make such calls as they think fit upon the members in respect of all moneys unpaid on the shares held by them respectively and not by the conditions of allotment thereof made payable at fixed times, and each member shall pay the amount of every call so made on him, to the persons and at the times and places appointed by the directors. A call may be made payable by instalments. A call shall be deemed to have been made at the time when the resolution of the directors authorizing such call was passed. No call shall be made exceeding one-fourth of the par value or a share or be made payable within months after days' notice shall be the last preceding call was payable. given specifying the time and place of payment, and to whom such call shall be paid. This notice shall be given in accordance with the by-laws of the company. If the sum payable in respect to any call or instalment shall not be paid on or before the pay appointed for the payment thereof, the holder for the time being of the share in respect to which the call shall have been made, or the instalment shall be due, shall pay interest for the same at the rate of per cent from the day appointed for payment thereof to the time of actual payment, or at such other rate as the board of directors may determine. The directors may, if they think fit, receive from any stockholder willing to advance the same all or any part of the moneys due upon the stock held by him in advance beyond the sums actually called for, and upon the stock so paid in advance dividends shall be paid proportional to the amount paid up. 

No. 56. Articles of Organization-Limitation on Amount of Stock 

Held.

No person, firm or company can ever at one time own or control more than shares of the capital stock of this company.

All meetings of the Stockholders shall be held at

Section 2. Annual Meeting. 

The annual meeting of the Stockholders shall be held on the of each year at day of and it shall be the duty of the secretary to give o'clock P. M. days notice of such meeting to each Stockholder personally or by mail, said notice to state the time and place of such meeting, and to be addressed to each Stockholder at his address as the same appears upon the records of the company; but failure to give notice shall not affect the validity of such meeting or proceedings thereat. At such meeting any business may be transacted not requiring a special notice.

Section 3. Special Meetings. 

Special meetings of the Stockholders may be held upon call by the Secretary when directed by the President or upon direction in writing of a majority of Directors then in office, or upon written direction of holders of not less than 

The Secretary shall give per cent of the outstanding stock. days notice of such meeting as specified in the preceding section, save that such notice shall, in addition, specify the purpose or purposes of the meeting. 

Section 4. Waiver of Notice of Meetings. 

A meeting of the Stockholders may regularly and validly be held whenever all members of the corporation shall be present at any meeting; however notified, and shall sign a written consent to the holding thereof upon the records; and at such meeting any business will be transacted which could lawfully be transacted at a meeting regularly called and notified. 

Section 5. Proxies and Voting. 

Each Stockholder may vote by proxy at any stockholders' meeting, and is entitled to one vote for each share of stock standing in his name upon the stockbook of the Company at the closing thereof for said meeting. Proxies must be filed with the secretary of the meeting before the same is adjourned.

Section 6. Quorum. 

Presence at any meeting, in person or by proxy, of Stockholders owning a majority of the stock of this corporation, shall constitute a quorum, save as otherwise provided by law; but less than a quorum, meeting at any time pursuant to notice, shall have power to adjourn from time to time until a quorum shall be present. 

Section 7. Conduct of Meetings. 

The President, or in his absence, the Vice President, shall preside at meetings of the Stockholders, and the Secretary shall act as secretary thereof; but should such officers not be present, their functions may be performed by any of the Stockholders present, as chosen by those in attendance.

ARTICLE II BOARD OF DIRECTORS Section 1. Powers. 

The Board of Directors shall have care and management of the stock, property, affairs and business of this corporation. Directors shall be elected annually by the Stockholders, at their annual meeting 367

No. 129a] 

WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS 

and from among their number, and shall hold office for year(s) or until their respective successors are chosen. 

The Board of Directors shall also have power, in addition to all others lawfully vested in them: (a) To purchase or otherwise acquire, lease, sell, convey, transfer or assign any property, rights, interests or privileges of the corporation, upon such terms and conditions, and for such price as such Board sees fit; and may, in its discretion, purchase or otherwise acquire property for the corporation, or agree to pay for services rendered or to be rendered to it, wholly or partially in the stock, bonds, or other evidences of indebtedness of the Company. (b) To elect or appoint assistants to the general officers, and to employ such servants and agents upon such terms and conditions as said Board may see fit, with power to remove or suspend any of the same, or all or any of the said general officers of the Company, and said Board may delegate to any officer of the Company by resolution, or to any committee of its members, all or any of the powers stated in this section, or any part of such powers. (c) To establish branch offices, factories, depots, or places or business for the carrying on of business at any place within this state, or elsewhere. (d) To authorize the borrowing of money for corporate purposes, as in the discretion of said Board seems fit, and for that purpose to execute or cause to be executed in the name of the Company such bills, notes or other evidences of debt as may be expedient. 

Section 2. Resignation of Directors. 

A director may resign at any time by filing a written resignation with the Secretary, and said resignation shall be effective from the filing thereof, unless a later date be fixed by its terms. 

Section 3. Removal of Directors. 

The Stockholders, at any special meeting called for such purpose, may remove from office any or all of the Directors, by the affirmative vote of the two holders of per cent of the outstanding stock.

Section 4. Filling of Vacancies. 

Vacancies on the Board of Directors, from any cause whatsoever, shall be filled by election by the Board of a successor or successors from among the qualified Stockholders of the Company, the person or persons so elected to serve until the next annual meeting of the Stockholders, or until a successor or successors is elected by the Stockholders. 368

Section 5. Meetings Generally. 

Meetings of the Board of Directors shall be held at 

Regular meetings shall be held

Special meetings shall be held upon call of the Secretary as directed by the President, or upon request of (state conditions); and the Secretary shall give notice of special meetings by (state mode). But meetings may be held at any time or place, all Directors being then and there in attendance and waiving notice and consenting to the holding thereof, and at such meetings any business may be transacted which could have been transacted had notice regularly been given. At any meeting of the 

Board, a majority of the existing Directors shall constitute a quorum for the transaction of business; but less than a majority may adjourn the meeting from time to time until a quorum shall be present. 

Section 6. Organization of Meetings and Order of Business. 

The President, and in his absence the Vice President, shall preside at meetings of the Board of Directors, and the Secretary shall act as secretary thereof; but in the absence of either or any of such officers, their functions may be performed by any member of the Board selected by those present. The regular order of business shall be: (1) Call of the roll; (2) Reading of minutes of previous meeting; (3) Reports of officers and committees; (4) Unfinished business; (5) New business.

Section 7. Interested Directors. 

Individual or personal interest of any Director in any matter which shall come before the Board of Directors shall not disqualify him from voting, or from being among the number requisite for a quorum at said meeting.

ARTICLE III GENERAL OFFICERS Section 1. Election. 

The President, Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer shall be elected annually at a regular meeting of the Board of Directors from the members of said Board, each of said general officers to hold office for the term of year(s) or until his successor is elected and qualifies.

Section 2. Duties of President. 

The President shall preside at all meetings of the Board of Directors or of the Stockholders. He is the chief executive officer of the Company, charged with its general supervision and management 369

No. 129a] WISCONSIN CORPORATIONS 

subject to the control of the Board of Directors, with the execution of contracts, deeds, leases, conveyances, and instruments generally on behalf of the corporation, and such other duties as may from time to time be prescribed by these by-laws or delegated to him by the 

Board of Directors. 

Section 3. Vice President. 

The Vice President shall discharge the duties of the President in his absence or disability, and, in addition, such other duties as may from time to time be prescribed by these by-laws or delegated to him by the Board of Directors. 

Section 4. Secretary. 

The Secretary shall keep a complete and permanent record of all proceedings of the Stockholders and of the Board of Directors. He shall, in addition, have general charge of the books and records of the corporation, except such as are hereinafter placed in charge of the Treasurer; shall countersign and seal with the seal of the corporation all instruments on behalf of the corporation; shall attend to the giving of notices of meetings of the Stockholders and of the Board of Directors; and shall, in addition, perform all such duties as may from time to time be imposed upon him by these by-laws or delegated to him by the Board of Directors. 

Section 5. Treasurer. 

The Treasurer shall be the fiscal and disbursing agent of the corporation. He shall keep and account for all moneys, credits and property; shall make and indorse checks and evidences of indebtedness; shall deposit funds coming to his possession in such depositories as may from time to time be designated by the Board of Directors; and shall, in addition, perform such other duties as may from time to time be vested in him by these by-laws, or delegated to him by the 

Board of Directors.

Section 6. Absence or Disability. 

In case of the absence or disability of any general officer of the corporation, the Board of Directors may delegate his duties to one of the other officers, or to a member of the Board of Directors, until the return or recovery of the absent or disabled officer.

ARTICLE IV CAPITAL STOCK 

Stock certificates shall be issued to each stockholder, representing the number of shares of the capital stock by him owned. Said cer- 370

ARTICLE V 

SEAL 

Section 1. Form and Custody. 

The Board of Directors shall adopt a seal for the corporation, which shall be in charge of the Secretary.

ARTICLE VI DIVIDENDS Section 1. In General. 

Dividends may be declared by the Board of Directors from time to time when and as there are net profits properly available therefor, payable either in cash or in stock of the corporation to record holders of the capital stock as shown by the stock book as hereinbefore provided.

ARTICLE VII CALLS AND ASSESSMENTS Section 1. Method of Making Call. 

Subscriptions to the capital stock of the corporation may be called in by the Board of Directors in such proportions and at such times as they see fit, by notice in writing mailed to each subscriber so liable not less than days prior to the date fixed for payment of said call, said notices to fix the time, place and terms of payment, to state the amount due, and to be mailed to subscribers by the Secretary at their last known addresses. 371

Whereas, the said

Company is indebted to sundry persons and corporations in a considerable amount for the construction, equipment and betterments of the plants, and is in need of funds for the purpose of paying such indebtedness, and also for the purpose of developing its plant and earning capacity, and placing it upon a dividend paying basis; and

Whereas, certain stockholders of said Company as a means and for the purpose of enabling said Company to raise and obtain the necessary funds to pay said indebtedness and to improve and develop its plant and earning capacity, heretofore donated and surrendered a certain percentage of the capital stock of said Company owned by them, and deposited the same in the hands of said and and as trustees and agents to sell the same for the benefit of said Company for a sum of not less than dollars; and

stock so deposited with them to the members of said syndicate for the sum of dollars, with the express understanding and agreement which was made a part of the consideration for the purchase and sale of said stock, and which understanding was and hereby is ratified by all of the parties hereto, that the stockholders of said Company owning a majority of the capital stock thereof would act together jointly and severally in the manner hereinafter set forth; and Whereas, the stockholders believe it to be essential to their interests to protect themselves against the purchase of a majority of the shares of the Company by parties acting on behalf of the corporate or other interests, to which the rights of the remaining stockholders would be subordinated, and also believe that it is essential for the success of said Company and for the best interest of all the stockholders thereof that the said Company shall be managed and directed during the next ten years of its existence under a definite and fixed policy to secure a union of all the interests in order properly to develop the rights, privileges, franchises, property and earning capacity of said Company; and

Whereas, they believe that their object can be best accomplished by acting together jointly and severally in the manner hereinafter set forth, the agreement of each constituting one of the considerations for the agreement of the others, and in particular by giving to the trustees as their agents and attorneys in fact an irrevocable power of sale upon the terms and conditions hereinafter set forth; and Whereas, for the purpose of this protection the stockholders have requested the trustees to take and hold for the period hereinafter stated the legal title to said shares, the same to be held by them upon an active trust, and to act under the terms of this agreement and the trustees have agreed so to do.

Ninth. The trustees covenant and agree to deposit with the depositary under this agreement the stock of the company owned or controlled by them respectively, and to take depositary's certificates therefor. Nothing herein contained shall deprive the trustees as individuals of the privilege to be enjoyed by all other depositors of selling or otherwise disposing of said certificates at their pleasure, or of purchasing additional certificates, or of purchasing additional stock and selling the same, or of joining in a syndicate to purchase under the power of sale herein given, at not less than the price herein named.

Tenth. The trustees shall not be entitled to any compensation for their services, but in case of a sale at not less than the price specified, the expenses and disbursement incurred by the trustees as such may be deducted from the proceeds to be distributed. 

Eleventh. In the event of the refusal or inability of the depositary hereinbefore named as depositary, to act as such depositary and registrar of the voting trust certificates distributed hereunder, the trustees shall have full power and authority to appoint another depositary and registrar to act hereunder in its place, and to authorize and arrange for the delivery by the retiring depositary to the depositary so appointed of all certificates of stock then held hereunder by the former. Upon the acceptance of such appointment the new depositary shall be clothed with all the power and control and be subject to all the duties and obligations hereby imposed upon the depositary herein named. Any depositary acting hereunder, and its or their successor, shall receive reasonable compensation for its and their services. Any depositary may resign its trust hereunder by giving thirty days' notice in writing of its intention so to do, which notice shall be directed to all and delivered to any one of the trustees then acting. In the event of such resignation a successor may be appointed by the trustees as hereinafter provided. 

Twelfth. Any trustee may at any time resign by delivering to the other trustees in writing his resignation to take effect ten days thereafter, and in every case of death, resignation or vacancy arising through other cause, the vacancy so occurring shall be filled by the appointment of the successor or successors to be made by the other 397
